Under severe pruning, diverse generated chain-of-thought (CoT) traces can coexist with increased repetition and less reliable generation. As correct answers become harder to sample, the additional attempts can sharply increase total token use even when individual responses become shorter. This separation between coverage and sampling efficiency also clarifies expert-selection gains, as methods with markedly different pass@1 can solve the same problems at large budgets yet require different numbers of attempts to reach a common coverage target. Pruning should therefore be assessed by both the range of problems a model can still solve and the sampling cost of obtaining correct solutions.
items.author: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng

items.title: CompSkill: Compiling Execution Experience for Skill Retrieval
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: https://github.com/satoshinji2992/CompSkill
items.author: Qi Shen, Ziyue Zhu, Yongqing Jiang, Zhen Xia, Li Shengjie, Shuai Zhao, Bo Cheng, Xiaobao Wu, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo

items.title: CogRSI: Evolving and Auditing Cognitive Reasoning Strategies
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can a language model learn better ways to reason about other people's minds by improving its own strategies, and are the strategies it learns actually right? We study this with cogrsi. A grounded reader marks who saw each event in a story and uses a short written principle to settle disagreements between its readings. With a principle written by experts, it beats self-consistency at the same token cost. A self-improvement loop then writes the principle itself. It keeps an update only if accuracy rises by a calibrated margin, and in one variant only if it also passes counterfactual test pairs. The learned principles transfer: on 800 BigToM pairs that no system had seen, each of them scores higher than the expert principle. We then check what the learned rules actually say. Each rule is translated into code and run on thousands of small stories with known answers. Most of them give a wrong answer in at least one situation they claim to cover, for example by treating a character who is in the room as knowing what happened even while asleep. Accuracy does not reveal which rules are wrong, and the counterfactual test does not fix this. A strategy can help in practice and still be wrong as a rule, so both need checking. Our code and data are publicly available.
items.author: Yandan zheng, Haoran Luo, Xinliang Zhou, Anhtuan Luu

items.title: Reformulation and Equivalence of Bock's Algorithm for Exact Dependency Parsing
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00939v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bock's algorithm provides a matrix-based alternative to Chu--Liu/Edmonds (CL/E) for exact dependency parsing. We present a reformulation that retains original node and arc identities through component labels, column adjustments, and star-and-bar transfers. In exact arithmetic, we prove operational equivalence to original Bock under matching scan and tie rules, and establish correspondence with corrected Tarjan under a prescribed component schedule. A separate analysis establishes optimal-value equivalence with Dozat-derived CL/E under the stated score and single-root conventions. We integrate reformulated Bock into a biaffine dependency parser and evaluate decoding and structured training on the Penn Treebank and Chinese Treebank. These results establish Bock as an alternative exact oracle for dependency parsing and structured training, while distinguishing equality of optimal values from identity of returned trees and training trajectories.
items.author: Yuxi Wang, Jungyeul Park

items.title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00883v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors. We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. The code and data are publicly available onhttps://github.com/George-Ling3/BestRand.
items.author: George Ling, Shanshan Zhong, Lijin Yang, Hao Yang, Nanxiang Li, Zhongzhan Huang

items.title: Steer, Don't Tell: Breaking Reasoning Plateaus with Reachability-Aligned Self-Distillation
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00796v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post training for large reasoning models remains insufficient on challenging problems, whose correct trajectories are hard to sample. Though prior works address this difficulty by integrating supervised fine tuning on expert trajectories with reinforcement learning, such external experts are not always available. Existing self improvement methods instead use reference solutions to create a privileged self-teacher. Yet privileged teacher correctness does not imply student reachability. Solution conditioning shifts the teacher distribution toward actions unlikely under the unprivileged student, producing seemingly "correct" trajectories that are unreachable or even mal-formed learning targets. Accordingly, we identify reachability alignment as the key to self constructed supervision and propose Self-Steered Reasoner (SSR). SSR realizes this principle through student support projection, which transforms the privileged teacher distribution into a directional signal only over reasoning actions locally reachable under the unguided student. Verification then retains correct trajectories sampled from this reachable space. To further boost the sampling efficiency, an iterative refinement framework is adopted, using diagnostic guidance based on current trajectories. On problems with pass@64 = 0 even after extensive RL, SSR recovers correct and learnable trajectories for 74.6% without parameter updates. Fine tuning on these trajectories followed by resumed reinforcement learning improves aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26. These results show that privileged guidance becomes effective self-improvement data when aligned with the reasoning actions the student can reach.
items.author: Zijian Wu, Lingkai Kong, Lin Yang, Haiteng Zhao, Kuikun Liu, Kai Chen, Dahua Lin, Wenwei Zhang

items.title: CheXPoT: Post-Hoc Visual Verification and Correction of VLM-Generated Radiology Reports
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise for chest radiograph report generation, but adoption remains limited because of hallucinated findings that are not grounded in the image. Correcting these hallucinations and improving overall report quality remains a significant challenge. Prior work has addressed this problem by refining models with reinforcement learning, preference optimization, or chain-of-thought supervision, often at substantial compute cost. To address this gap, we introduce CheXPoT, a program-of-thought (PoT) framework that verifies each generated finding against image features and removes those it cannot ground. CheXPoT decomposes generated reports into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, grounds these predicates against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table, executes PoT verification code, and rewrites reports after removing unsupported predicates. On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 19.2% (MedGemma-4B) to 46.8% (MedGemma-4B + CheXPoT) and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%, absolute gains of 27.6% and 26.4% respectively. We also tested CheXPoT on other VLM report generators. On LLaVA-Med, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 4.5% to 17.7% and micro-average F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%. On MAIRA-2, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 15.6% to 42.1% and micro-average F1 from 21.0% to 45.3%. Our results suggest that inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve VLM trustworthiness by correcting unsupported findings from generated reports. CheXPoT lays a foundation for tools that help validate VLM-generated radiology reports and reduce unsupported findings. These innovations may subsequently help increase trust and adoption of VLM tools in Medicine.
items.author: Joey Guo, Rayan Ansari, Alaa Youssef

items.title: DuSE-Bench: Benchmarking Joint Reasoning over Evolving Dialogue and Documents
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00755v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Persistent Web information assistants must combine evolving document facts with user requirements established and revised across sessions. Yet systematic evaluation of how changes in both sources affect response requirements and evidence attribution remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce Dual-Source Evolution Benchmark (DuSE-Bench), a benchmark comprising 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 whose required premises originate in both dialogue and documents. An evolving Support Graph guides task construction and preserves links from updated facts and reused conclusions to original turns and passages. Task annotations distinguish grounding source from state dependence and enable separate evaluation of response content, response type, and source attribution. Experiments across 11 baseline configurations reveal persistent challenges in joint reasoning over evolving dialogue and documents, with content accuracy on jointly grounded tasks reaching at most 56.7%. Moreover, improvements in content accuracy can coincide with poorer response choice, while content-correct responses frequently lack complete attribution to original evidence. Matched evidence substitutions further show that the effect of replacing one source's evidence depends on support from the other. These findings motivate coordinating dialogue memory and document retrieval to apply current user requirements and document facts together while preserving their original support. The data are available at https://github.com/JianfengGao7/DuSE-Bench.
items.author: Guanjie Cheng, Jianfeng Gao, Yufei Tong, Xinkui Zhao, Shuiguang Deng

items.title: Constructing Budgeted KGW Evasion through Token-Event Evidence Replacement
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00726v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: KGW watermarks bias sampling to accumulate keyed detection evidence. We construct budgeted evasion through token-event evidence replacement using ordinary phrase rewrites. Our construction jointly selects compositions of LLM-proposed alternatives from an independent model and measures global token-edit distance on complete outputs. At the largest attainable cost within the budget, exact coverage search maximizes removal of original scored token pairs. It uses a known tokenizer without the key, detector feedback or queries to the watermarked model. Exact accounting separates source evidence removed, evidence created and length effects, with initial strength setting the required reduction. Separate signed-event analysis found that mean suppression arose mainly from removing watermark-enriched source events. In controlled, occurrence-counted, one-token-context KGW tests on short passages, 39 of 82 qualified, initially detected sources yielded rewrites with terminal detector score Z < 4 that passed blinded source-relative model review, at a mean actual token-edit cost of 16.0% under a 20% allowance. To examine whether this initial requirement can be inferred, a separate historical 95-passage study estimated initial detector score Z0 from generation traces with correlation 0.793 and an in-sample association beyond length. This aggregate information did not establish improved allocation, and the separate no-trace stopping test did not reliably exploit cheaper reviewed crossings in the candidate bank. Comparisons did not establish an advantage over simpler selection and ordinary constrained rewriting. The construction makes budgeted evidence replacement executable while exposing limits in signed reduction and recognition of sufficient editing.
items.author: Hongliang Liu

items.title: Enhancing Language Model Reasoning with Structured Multi-Level Modeling
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00616v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inference-time scaling enhances a model's reasoning by extending its chain-of-thought (CoT). However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.
items.author: Siheng Xiong, Ali Payani, Faramarz Fekri

items.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large: Fine-Tuning a 560M Embedder for Tajik Retrieval
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00592v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Finding the passage that answers a question is the first step of most practical systems built on documents, and for Tajik we found no openly described model for it. We present Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large, a Tajik text embedder built from multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M parameters). We asked our own Tajik language model to write questions for passages from Tajik laws, tax documents, Wikipedia and web text, and trained on 235,140 question and passage pairs for one epoch, with hard negatives chosen by another embedder and English and Russian pairs mixed in so the model would not forget those languages. On laws the model had never seen, the right passage is among the top ten results for 93.6% of questions, up from 80.2%; on tax documents, 94.5% against 82.6%. On Belebele, the one test we have that was written by people, the gain is smaller and not confirmed (92.2% to 95.2%, with touching intervals), and Russian and English do not change. On law and tax questions written in the same style as its training questions, it is tied with Giga-Embeddings-3B, a model five times its size; on Belebele the 3B and 8B models score slightly higher, and only after we fine-tuned them on our data are they clearly ahead. We also report what failed: training in bfloat16 broke the model, and replacing Tajik letters with similar Russian ones did not help. Our law, tax and Wikipedia test questions come from the same model that wrote the training questions, so we treat those scores as an upper limit until questions written by Tajik speakers are available.
items.author: Tohir Saidzoda, Nekruz Maxudov, Bedil Karimov, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva

items.title: From Apparent Search Gains to Selection Failures: Auditing Test-Time Inference in Structured Workflow Planning
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00579v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time search can improve structured planning, but when methods differ in prompts, post-processing, and selection, it is unclear what an observed gain should be attributed to. We study this question on DisasterBench, where models compose typed multi-tool workflows, by decomposing inference into three observable stages: whether a correct workflow is discovered, whether it survives structural validation, and whether it is finally selected. Comparing independent sampling, a nominal tree-search configuration, and multi-operator search under controlled inference budgets on two model families, we find that (i) the nominal tree-search configuration realizes non-adaptive complete-workflow sampling, and independent sampling with its expansion prompt reproduces its candidate discovery without constructing a tree; (ii) structural validation never removes the last correct workflow in our evaluated candidate pools, whereas majority voting leaves a discovered correct workflow unselected on 10-19% of tasks per pool, with an audit confirming substantive tool-choice or information-flow errors in 57 of 60 examined cases; and (iii) a tool-specification-aware verifier recovers some of these losses but overturns more correct decisions than it fixes. Our results motivate auditing realized rather than nominal inference pipelines, and reporting discovery, validity, and selection separately.
items.author: Zhitong Chen, Weifeng Zhang, Kai Yin, Zhiyuan Wang, Ali Mostafavi, James Caverlee

items.title: Distinguishing among reasoning levels of GPT 5.5 Pro via a grammar lens benchmark
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00555v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Does the level of test-time processing effort affect a language model's computational capability? A formal grammar-lens benchmark method, derived from the theory of computation, generates novel data at specified levels, each successively more computationally powerful than the levels below. Using this data, we tested GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.5-Pro-Medium, -High, and -XHigh, showing incrementally increased acceptance of test data: 16, 40, 43, and 52\%, respectively, illustrating the benchmark's ability to discern fine-grained differences among models' added test-time reasoning levels. Additionally, as test-time compute effort increases, model responses diverge from human responses to the same data. This increasing disagreement may turn out to be broadly characteristic of more capable language models, introducing the potential of a general capability-versus-alignment conflict.
items.author: Emma Graham, Richard Granger

items.title: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment: A Benchmark for Policy-Change Reasoning
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. We propose Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE), which evaluates an ordered pair of policy directives on both dimensions at once: a binary judgment determines whether the two directives govern the same policy domain, and a five-way judgment determines whether the later directive continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses the earlier policy, or governs a different domain altogether. Read together, the two judgments form one five-category label, our primary metric. The two-axis design captures two central dimensions of policy change without conflating errors on either dimension into a generic "irrelevant" label, and it makes annotation more rigorous: a coder cannot dismiss a difficult pair as domain-irrelevant without an explicit, checkable decision. We introduce an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 ordered directive pairs drawn from a large corpus of Chinese government policy, together with an annotation-calibration protocol (an adjudication packet with pre/post agreement measurement) that we contribute as a methodological artifact. Fourteen open-weight models and four frontier API flagships fail the task zero-shot: even the best frontier flagship's chance-corrected agreement with expert labels is far below the human ceiling (Cohen's $\kappa \approx 0.29$ vs. $0.53$). A fine-tuned open-weight model (LoRA SFT of Qwen3-14B, five-fold cross-validation) closes this gap, reaching the coder-mutual human ceiling ($\kappa = 0.524$ vs. $0.527$). Finally, we apply our method to China's AI policy (1980-2024) and map the direction of policy change across eras.
items.author: Charles Chang (Duke Kunshan University), Yuen Yuen Ang (Johns Hopkins University), Bolun Sun (Northwestern University)

items.title: Steering Readerly Dynamics: Trajectory-Guided Story Generation with Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00469v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate stories, but these stories struggle to reproduce engaging readerly dynamics, the evolving reader responses that shape narrative experience. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that learns readerly dynamics from high-quality human-written stories and uses them to guide story generation. Instead of directly modeling high-dimensional story content, we train a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories. We then leverage the strong instruction-following capability of a larger, off-the-shelf writer LLM to generate story segments that follow these predicted trajectories within a given story setting. Our framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.
items.author: Danrui Li, Yiwei Zhao, Mubbasir Kapadia, Lingxiao Li

items.title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00420v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribution graphs, an emerging tool in mechanistic interpretability, use transcoders to decompose language model computations into sparse interpretable features connected by causal edges. However, turning a graph into a safety-relevant insight requires hours of manual analysis by experts. We introduce Circuit Oracle, an off-the-shelf LLM equipped with a multi-agent harness and task-specific authored skills, which answers natural-language questions about a target model by reading the attribution graph through tool calls. We evaluate it on three safety-relevant proxy tasks: detecting spurious features in probe circuits, eliciting hidden knowledge from taboo-finetuned models, and suppression jailbreaking via feature-level interventions. Beyond task scores, the oracle produces pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature explanations that we assess qualitatively. Results are mixed. On spurious-feature detection, Circuit Oracle reaches 78.2 $\pm$ 2.4% accuracy, outperforming single-layer feature-ranking baselines. On secret elicitation, trained self-explainers like Activation Oracles remain the stronger baseline. On refusal suppression over 50 prompts, its single committed intervention is slightly below a diff-in-means baseline, and only exceeds it when allowed the best of five attempts. Results are stable across five runs and across model choices for the agents. We also release the pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature readings that revise existing global labels, and invite future work to develop evaluations that can measure their usefulness directly.
items.author: Shariar Kabir, Hong Kiat Tan, Swastik Agrawal, Sai V R Chereddy, Sriram Balasubramanian

items.title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00359v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.
items.author: Ziyuan Wang, Genliang Zhu, Xiaobo Chen

items.title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00345v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.
items.author: Organizers of QueerInAI,  :, A Pranav, Alissa A. Valentine, Alex Markham, Beckett LeClair, Tereza Blazkova, Ekaterina Kornilitsina, Sofie H. Bruun, Gerasimos Spanakis, Anne Lauscher

items.title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.
items.author: Rajdeep Pal, Jotiraditya Banerjee, Saptarshi Pani

items.title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00300v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.
items.author: Saehee Eom, Tejas Khandwekar

items.title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.
items.author: Yunfan Zhang, Taehoon Hwang, Kathleen McKeown, Smaranda Muresan

items.title: On the Error Analysis of Triangular Transport Maps for Conditional Generation via MMD-based Objectives
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.33610v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Conditional generative models parameterized by triangular transport maps are widely used for conditional sampling, yet theoretical guarantees on the quality of the conditional measures they produce remain scarce. We address this question for minimum divergence estimators of triangular maps. We use MMD-based objectives as a tractable setting in which the gap between joint and conditional errors can be analyzed precisely, and we measure performance through the average conditional estimation error, defined as the squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the estimated and the true conditionals, averaged over the conditioning variable. We first show that the common practice of minimizing a joint MMD may fail to recover the conditionals: writing the joint and the conditional criteria as quadratic energies of the same conditional mean embedding residual, we prove that, for parametric classes, joint minimizers are generically inconsistent in the misspecified setting. We then analyze an estimator that directly minimizes the conditional criterion through a surrogate loss computable from joint target samples and reference samples. We prove a non-asymptotic error bound that decomposes the average conditional estimation error into approximation, estimation, and reference sampling errors, with fast rates independent of the ambient dimension in the parametric setting. Finally, for joint MMDs built from concentrating Gaussian kernels on the conditioning variable, we show that the joint criterion approximates a density-reweighted version of the conditional one, and we derive an error bound for the joint minimizer whose rate suffers from a curse of dimensionality in the conditioning variable. Our results suggest that training criteria for conditional generative models should target the conditional rather than the joint error, a principle that extends to other divergences and to dynamic transport.
items.author: Michele Martino, Bamdad Hosseini, Amir Sagiv, Amirhossein Taghvaei

items.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.27606v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $\epsilon$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.
items.author: Kaicheng Zhang, Hongqian Niu, Laixi Shi, Didong Li, Guannan Qu, Zhun Deng

items.title: Lower Bounds for Stochastic First-Order Algorithms with Variance Reduction in Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Optimization
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.01662v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We establish complexity lower bounds for stochastic first-order algorithms in nonconvex--concave minimax optimization, allowing algorithms to use variance reduction. Our main contribution is a lower bound for a zero-respecting algorithm class that permits variance reduction, extending beyond the algorithmic restrictions imposed by some existing lower bounds. We consider objectives with an $L$-Lipschitz continuous joint gradient, a compact convex dual domain of Euclidean radius at most $D_Y$, and a primal value function, defined by maximizing the objective over the dual variable, with initial suboptimality at most $\Delta$. The target accuracy $\varepsilon$ is measured by the gradient norm of the Moreau envelope of the constrained primal value function with parameter $1/(2L)$. Under an unbiased stochastic first-order oracle with variance at most $\sigma^2$ and mean-squared smoothness, we prove the lower bound $\Omega\!\left(L^2D_Y\Delta\varepsilon^{-3}+L^3D_Y^2\Delta\sigma^2\varepsilon^{-6}\right)$. This result quantifies the dependence on accuracy, dual-domain radius, and oracle noise even when variance reduction is allowed. We also establish complementary lower bounds for nonconvex--strongly-concave minimax optimization. With dual strong-concavity parameter $\mu>0$ and condition number $\kappa:=L/\mu$, we obtain $\Omega\!\left(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}+L\Delta\kappa\sigma^2\varepsilon^{-4}\right)$ under the bounded-variance oracle model. Under the additional mean-squared smoothness condition with constant $\bar L$, we obtain $\Omega\!\left(L\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon^{-2}+\Delta\bar L\sigma\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}\right)$. Together, these results identify complexity barriers across the concave and strongly concave regimes, with the main nonconvex--concave bound remaining valid for algorithms that use variance reduction.
items.author: Jiayi Song, Zi Xu

items.title: Component-Weighted Centroid Search for Exact Incremental BPE
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.40016v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Exact incremental tokenizers keep the tokenization of a growing text up to date, so a long prompt or agent trace is not retokenized each time it grows. Jiang and Gong's algorithm does this for byte-pair encoding (BPE) in $O(\log^2 t)$ worst-case time per byte, where $t$ is the length of the longest token. Its search passes through $O(\log t)$ nested subproblems and runs a binary search over the possible branches at each one. We weight each branch by the size of the subproblem it leads to. Each step then costs about one probe for every halving of the remaining candidates, and a whole update costs $O(\log t)$, as much as one binary search over all candidates. Output and asymptotic memory are unchanged. We also construct valid BPE vocabularies on which the original search provably needs $\Theta(\log^2 t)$ probes and ours $\Theta(\log t)$, and a Rust implementation reproduces both counts exactly. On six real vocabularies the two searches run at about the same speed on ordinary text, while on long runs of spaces or hyphens the weighted search is up to 2.5$\times$ faster.
items.author: Harshit Verma, Rex Ying

items.title: Schr\"odinger--F\"ollmer Actor--Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.33239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions, but a $Q$-weighted update does not specify how to sample from the resulting target distribution. We propose Schr\"odinger--F\"ollmer Actor--Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) method for Kullback--Leibler (KL)-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. A minimax Bellman critic estimates the action-value function, which defines an exponentially tilted target policy. A Doob $h$-transform expresses this update as a correction to the reference diffusion drift. The target drift is a weighted conditional mean of Brownian-bridge labels. We fit it by weighted regression using endpoints from the current policy and pointwise action-value evaluations. In the small-update regime, the KL-regularized update follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds that separate the errors from critic estimation, weighted neural drift regression, and diffusion discretization through a reverse-KL actor bound. The average-performance bound depends explicitly on the comparison coefficients over the policy iterations. Synthetic experiments assess approximation to prescribed advantage-tilted targets and sensitivity to the diffusion-step count. Across six offline-to-online continuous-control tasks, the $Q$-guided bridge-regression implementation achieves higher final-checkpoint returns than its BC initialization after $500K$ online interactions.
items.author: Yuling Jiao, Lican Kang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Jincheng Ying

items.title: Learning Steadily: Accumulating Relative Point Margin Scores for Face Image Quality Assessment
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.31662v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Face Image Quality Assessment determines the suitability of captured face images for automated face recognition (FR), a critical capability for reliable biometric systems. Existing state-of-the-art FR-integrated FIQA methods suffer from temporal instability: as the feature space evolves during training, single-epoch quality estimates fluctuate, creating a moving target that undermines reliable quality prediction. We introduce CARPM-FIQA, a stabilization strategy for FR-integrated FIQA that accumulates relative point margin measurements, the ratio between intra-class compactness and inter-class separation, across the entire training trajectory rather than relying on single-epoch estimates. This cumulative averaging approach provides theoretically grounded advantages: reduced variance in quality estimates, improved mean squared error, and enhanced ranking stability with convergence guarantees as training progresses. Through controlled experiments on the SynFIQA dataset with labeled quality groups, we demonstrate that cumulative averaging achieves superior discriminative ability, and ablation studies across different training configurations confirm consistent improvements. Evaluated against twelve FIQA methods on eight challenging benchmarks with four FR models at two FMR thresholds, CARPM-FIQA places 4th (CARPM-FIQA(L)) and 6th (CARPM-FIQA(S)) of 17 compared methods by pAUC-EDC and AUC-EDC averaged across FR models and, after per-benchmark normalization, across benchmarks, staying within a few percent of the best method's normalized average for every FR model, providing a principled solution to training instability while maintaining the performance benefits of FR integration. More broadly, our work demonstrates that temporal aggregation strategies can stabilize training objectives in deep learning systems where target values inherently fluctuate due to evolving feature representations.
items.author: Guray Ozgur, Tahar Chettaoui, Eduarda Caldeira, Marco Huber, Jan Niklas Kolf, Naser Damer, Fadi Boutros

items.title: Nonparametric In-Context Learning under Growing Geometric Complexity: Minimax Optimality and Local Geometry-Adaptivity of Transformers
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.31458v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Transformers have become a central architecture for in-context learning (ICL), particularly through their state-of-the-art performance in large language models. This success motivates understanding how transformers exploit intrinsic geometry of real-world data. However, existing nonparametric ICL theory has largely focused on simplified settings, such as Euclidean domains or single manifold models, failing to fully explain its phenomenal empirical success in complex tasks. To address this gap, we study the prediction problem under unknown heterogeneous geometry, modeled by sample size-dependent mixtures of manifolds with heterogeneous dimensions, smoothness, and sampling masses. Under the growing geometric complexity model, we establish a minimax lower bound capturing the aggregate difficulty of the components and construct an oracle tangent local polynomial estimator with a matching upper bound. This estimator is connected to a structure-informed, two-stage softmax transformer with a geometric preconditioner and local polynomial solvers. The transformer achieves negligible approximation error relative to the minimax rate with logarithmic depth and polynomial size. Finally, we derive an in-context generalization bound for near empirical risk minimizers (ERM) over this class. Together, these results identify conditions under which the resulting predictor exploits local geometry and attains minimax rate.
items.author: Jaehee Seo, Jisu Kim

items.title: Learning a Flow to Self-Supervised Representations
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.29350v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce Flow-Based Distribution Matching (FBDM), which learns self-supervised representations through non-adversarial velocity regression. The encoder and auxiliary field are trained jointly by regressing analytic velocities along spherical paths from learned representations to reference targets. Both augmented views share a reference target, with a capacity limit on each reference center and an explicit view-alignment loss. A structured reference supports more components than the auxiliary flow dimension while retaining geometric separation. The auxiliary field is discarded after pretraining; only the backbone is retained downstream. On three ResNet-18 benchmarks with matched auxiliary parameter counts, FBDM provides 2.17 to 2.36 times higher per-epoch training throughput than critic-based Distribution Matching (DM), with about 0.21 GiB additional peak allocated GPU memory. Experiments show that FBDM is competitive with existing SSL methods from CIFAR to ImageNet and performs comparably to DM on their shared benchmarks. Under stated conditions, our population analysis bounds nearest-centroid classification error on the initial normalized pretraining representation by the FBDM loss.
items.author: Yuling Jiao, Wensen Ma, Houduo Qi, Defeng Sun

items.title: Conformal Bayes under Continuous Label Shift: Sensitivity Analysis and the Limits of Exact Validity
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.27976v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Conformal Bayes combines Bayesian posterior predictive scores with conformal calibration. Under continuous label shift, both the score and calibration weights depend on an unknown response density ratio. Existing methods typically estimate a single exponential tilt from pseudo-labels or predictive samples and plug it into calibration. We propose Joint Tilt-Sensitivity Conformal Bayes (JTS-CB), which performs sensitivity analysis over a prespecified family of tilts. Each tilt defines a coupled score-weight pair. The split procedure, JTS-SCB, solves joint min-max calibration by taking the largest tilt-specific threshold from weighted intercept-only quantile regression. JTS-Union retains individual thresholds, yielding prediction sets contained in those of JTS-SCB. Both use calibration-only weights by design, without a general coverage guarantee. We also study a candidate-weighted exact counterpart. Any nonzero linear exponential tilt makes its prediction set unbounded, whereas compact negative-quadratic families yield bounded exact unions under Gaussian scores. For the practical procedures, a localized correction with fallback gives coverage at least nominal minus a target tail-mass bound when the family contains the true tilt, but can substantially increase width. Experiments on controlled shifts of three regression datasets and on synthetic data show that plug-in predictive sampling can approach oracle coverage when the shift is well identified, but remains vulnerable to predictive bias and unstable tilt estimation. Sensitivity analysis can mitigate these failures in the tested settings, at the cost of wider prediction sets. Coupling scores and weights can yield narrower sets with higher coverage than varying weights alone, although this advantage is not uniform across shifts. Excluding the true tilt from the sensitivity family can still cause undercoverage.
items.author: Seungjin Choi

items.title: Domain-decomposed Evolutional Deep Neural Network with Random Features for Transient Pressure Diffusion with Discontinuous and High-Contrast Coefficients
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.22349v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Transient pressure diffusion in heterogeneous porous media becomes difficult to resolve efficiently when permeability is discontinuous and spans several orders of magnitude. In this paper, we develop a domain-decomposed random-feature evolutional deep neural network (DD RF-EDNN) that separates spatial approximation from temporal evolution. Permeability-informed random features are compressed into an orthonormal pressure space, and a conservative finite-volume operator is projected onto this space so that only the reduced coordinates are advanced in time. This formulation retains the dissipative structure of the discrete flow problem without repeated neural-network optimization. The analysis quantifies dictionary and singular-value truncation errors, proves contractivity under an energy-consistent dissipativity correction, and derives a conditional grid-level estimate for homogeneous dynamics and time-independent data admitting a steady lifting. Numerical experiments on low-permeability inclusions, high-conductivity blocks and channels, and three-dimensional grids assess the accuracy of the method across distinct coefficient configurations. The method reaches a final-time relative $L^2$ error of $9.54\times10^{-4}$ in the principal benchmark and maintains errors on the order of $10^{-2}$ at a permeability contrast of $10^3$. Numerical diagnostics further show that the observed error balance and temporal convergence are consistent with the analysis. These results support DD RF-EDNN as a structure-preserving and interpretable reduced formulation for transient simulations on prescribed heterogeneous media.
items.author: Peiqi Li, Jie Chen, Hui Zhang, Simon Hands

items.title: Low-Rank Denoising for Predict-then-Optimize
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.15111v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A shortest-path decision is often made from edge costs that are only observed through noisy samples, such as the average of $m$ simulation replications. When the mean cost vectors of different instances lie near a $k$-dimensional subspace, projecting the averaged sample onto that subspace should remove noise. We make this precise. The mean squared error of any projection estimator splits exactly into a variance term and a bias term. The best projector is the positive eigenspace of $\Sigma_c - D/m$, where $\Sigma_c$ is the covariance of the true costs and $D$ is the noise covariance. For a rank-$k$ signal, the projection has the error of a sample mean with a factor $d/(\mu k)$ more replications, where $d$ is the number of edges and $\mu$ is an incoherence constant. For a signal that is only approximately low-rank, every rank-$k$ projection has an error floor, and the plain average wins beyond an explicit replication count. A margin bound shows that the chance of choosing a suboptimal path falls at the same improved rate. A projector learned from $n$ noisy instances loses at most an $O(d/n)$ term.
items.author: Henry Aldridge-Krawciw, Irene Aldridge

items.title: The Platonic brain bridge hypothesis: brain networks as architectural priors for multimodal large language models
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.10947v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models predict brain activity, but brain alignment has been a measurement, not a design tool. We propose the Platonic brain bridge hypothesis: omni models, multimodal large language models that process video, audio and text jointly, converge on brain-like representations usable in both directions. From model to brain, brain-likeness of seven omni models is stable across participants, rises with every input channel in three bases, and our encoders lead the Algonauts 2025 out-of-distribution leaderboard. From brain to model, Brain-MoE fixes the expert partition of a frozen base to the seven networks of human cortex, trains experts on network-labelled Brain-AVQA questions, raises held-out accuracy in all 15 model-benchmark pairs by 6.42 percentage points on average and exceeds capacity-matched random experts in 14. Brain-Scope localizes the correspondence to sparse features whose removal weakens brain prediction. Human brain organization is therefore a usable architectural prior for multimodal large language models.
items.author: Pengfei Zhang, Biao Tian, Xiangang Li, Hui Xiong, Li Liu

items.title: Minimax Rate for Diffusion-Guided Local Intrinsic Dimension Estimation based on Fokker-Planck Equation
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.04822v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Diffusion-guided methods have recently emerged as effective tools for probing the intrinsic geometry of high-dimensional data. Understanding their accuracy requires quantifying both (i) finite-scale approximation error relative to the true local intrinsic dimension (LID) and (ii) estimation error from finite samples. We address these two questions for the FLIPD field (Kamkari et al., 2024; arXiv:2406.03537), defined at the population level through the logarithmic scale derivative of a Gaussian-smoothed density and admitting a Fokker--Planck representation. For $\alpha$-smooth densities on a regular $d$-dimensional manifold, we establish a uniform $O(\sigma^2)$ approximation bound relative to the manifold dimension $d$. Under expected integrated squared loss, we prove a minimax lower bound of order $(n\sigma^d)^{-1}$ for estimating the FLIPD field from $n$ observations when $n^{-1/(2\alpha+d)}\le\sigma\le\sigma_0$. A plug-in FLIPD estimator based on the empirical denoising score matching (DSM) solution attains a matching upper bound. Thus the minimax rate is of order $(n\sigma^d)^{-1}$ and it becomes $n^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d)}$ at its smallest scale.
items.author: Jaehee Seo, Wontae Jeong, Jisu Kim

items.title: The Price of Intelligence: A Quality-Adjusted Price Index for AI Services
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.29843v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: How fast AI inference prices have fallen depends on how an index holds quality constant. We build quality-adjusted price indices for text and code inference sold through APIs, joining 21,024 posted prices to a capability scale fitted to 4,605 benchmark scores. From January 2025 to July 2026, matched-model methods record an annual fall of 0.07 in log price per token. Our pre-specified hedonic index falls at 0.51 a year in logs (95% interval 0.11 to 0.89), entirely through the rising capability of the models on sale. Across three treatments of measurement error and two anchor sets it runs from 0.34 to 0.89. Excluding six anchors flagged for possible contamination leaves model rankings intact (rank correlation 0.998) yet lowers the rate by 0.40 to 0.51 under two treatments. Agreement on rankings therefore does not license claims about levels or increments. Per completed task, the data do not establish a quality-adjusted decline.
items.author: Louis Yiven Zhu

items.title: Item-Mean Surrogates: Why Richer Personas Fail to Deliver Individual Fidelity in LLMs as Human Surrogates
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.29455v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used to simulate and study human behavior. Such studies assume richer personas improve predictions of specific people's answers. We test this premise across four public datasets. First, we split each person's answer to an item into the item mean (the average human answer to that item) and the person's deviation from the item mean. Much of the accuracy that surrogate studies report comes from predicting item means. LLM predictions explain little of the deviations. We call this pattern item-mean surrogacy. Second, we split each deviation into stable signal and noise using a dataset in which the same participants answered the same questions twice. Stable signal is the part of a deviation that repeated answers share. Noise is the part that changes. In this dataset, more than half of the variance in deviations persists across occasions. Most of what the LLM misses is stable signal rather than noise. Third, we split stable signal into the person signal, a person's average deviation across questions, and the person-by-item signal, their remaining question-specific deviations. The person-by-item signal accounts for about 8.5 times as much variance as the person signal. The LLM recovers about a tenth of it. Richer personas, different models, and fine-tuning on human answers still leave most of the person-by-item signal unrecovered. Both fine-tuned models recover less of this signal than their untuned versions. These findings call for closer empirical scrutiny of LLMs as human surrogates.
items.author: Daehwan Ahn, Chengfeng Mao, Dokyun Lee

items.title: Offline Deep Q* Estimation with Diffusion Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.14401v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In offline RL, estimating the optimal action-value function $Q^*$ can be formulated as solving the optimal Bellman equation based solely on offline observations. A fundamental challenge is that the reward function and transition kernel are unknown, so the optimal Bellman operator is not directly observable from data. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that decouples operator estimation from value function learning. In this approach, we first formulate conditional diffusion models to estimate the reward law and transition kernel, which induces a data-driven approximation of the optimal Bellman operator. We then plug these estimators into the Bellman equation and obtain a deep estimator of $Q^*$ by minimizing the empirical Bellman residual over a neural network function class. Theoretically, we first establish sharp nonasymptotic convergence rates for learning the optimal Bellman operator. We establish the smoothness of $Q^*$ through the Bellman equation using the the H\"older assumptions on the conditional reward and transition densities. With suitable sample sizes, we obtain the oracle value-stage rate $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\bigl(n^{-\frac{2\alpha}{d_x+d_a+2\alpha}}\bigr)$ for the excess Bellman residual risk. We then translate this risk bound into an expected $L^2$ estimation error of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\bigl(n^{-\frac{\alpha}{d_x+d_a+2\alpha}}\bigr)$ under a concentrability condition. For the total offline budget $\widetilde n=n+n_r+n_x$, we obtain a value estimation rate of $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\bigl(\widetilde n^{-\frac{\alpha}{2d_x+d_a+2\alpha}}\bigr)$ and establish an information-theoretic lower bound of order $\widetilde n^{-\frac{\alpha}{d_x+d_a+2\alpha}}$. Importantly, our theoretical analysis does not rely on Bellman completeness assumptions commonly used in deep RL theory.
items.author: Xiaohong Chen, Yuling Jiao, Lican Kang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Chen Zhong

items.title: Consilience for Verifier-Free Test-Time Scaling
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.09898v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Test-time scaling often uses an external verifier, such as compilers and test cases in coding or trained value functions in robotics applications, to obtain high-quality rollouts. Verifier-free test-time scaling (or VF-TTS) is gaining extensive attention as a mechanism to enhance Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning, primarily because we do not have access to such high-quality verifiers in many real-world applications. Among existing VF-TTS methods, confidence-based VF-TTS methods, which compute and rank rollouts solely by confidence, are particularly promising. Such methods introduce near-zero overhead for sample evaluation and require minimal access to internal model states, making the methods highly flexible across models and tasks.
  In this paper, we demonstrate a critical limitation of existing confidence-based VF-TTS methods by showing that such methods catastrophically break down on complex tasks. We observe a very interesting phenomenon: uniformly high confidence frequently indicates a failure to explore, favoring confidently wrong answers. To address this, our core insight is that robust cognitive search requires a specific confidence trajectory pattern: such methods perform exploratory branching at the beginning, as manifested by low initial confidence, and converge to a high final confidence solution. To implement this insight, we introduce consilience, a novel selection framework that explicitly evaluates the temporal asymmetry of confidence in reasoning. We operationalize this via a combinatorial metric that actively penalizes high initial confidence while strictly demanding final certainty. Extensive experiments covering both graduate-level mathematics problems and free-form code generation demonstrate that consilience effectively outperforms existing baselines, validating our novel perspective on completion confidence.
items.author: Lecheng Kong, Like Hui, Haitao Mao, Jun Huan

items.title: AgentSnare: Learning to Delay, Divert, and Defuse Autonomous Web Penetration Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.26998v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language model agents automate web penetration testing through observation-action loops, enabling defenders to influence decisions with deceptive decoy observations. Advanced agents can recognize and bypass static decoys, then refocus on real targets. We propose AgentSnare, a trajectory-adaptive deception system that expands a decoy environment alongside exploration. For online deployment, ShadowOS combines an LLM-driven decoy constructor with a virtual kernel. Conditioned on exploration, it generates decoy artifacts that the kernel materializes and handles consistently across interactions, sustaining long-horizon exploration. Because deploying a powerful LLM for decoy construction is costly and slow, we train a small LLM using an offline adversarial interaction-simulation framework. It synthesizes multi-round trajectories by generating candidates and retaining those that sustain simulated interactions. Across 15 CVE-Bench web applications and four attacker models, AgentSnare absorbs 49.9% of tool calls to delay attacks, retains 57.2% of post-entry actions in the decoy to divert trajectories, and grounds 89.5% of completion reports in decoy evidence to defuse threats; across 60 attacker-CVE pairs, no real target is exploited at pass@3.
items.author: Ruoyu Wang, Heng Zhao, Renjie Wu, Tianhang Zheng, Mengnan Zhao, Wanyu Lin, Kui Ren

items.title: Kernel Ridge Regression over H\"older Classes: Function and Derivative Losses
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.26065v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study ordinary kernel ridge regression over full H\"older-Zygmund balls, measuring errors in Sobolev norms and in pointwise and uniform losses for mixed derivatives. For targets of smoothness $s$, every RKHS norm equivalent to $H^{s+d/2}$ gives the optimal $H^r$ risk for $0\le r<s$; integer choices of $r$ include integrated squared derivative losses. Pointwise and uniform guarantees require additional kernel structure. A localized wavelet kernel attains the sharp derivative rates with the same regularization orders as for function estimation, whereas equivalent changes of the RKHS norm can destroy the population bias rates. For the ordinary Gaussian kernel with a shrinking bandwidth, we prove a uniform derivative risk bound with the optimal polynomial rate and an explicit, unoptimized logarithmic factor. The results allow bounded measurable design densities bounded away from zero and conditionally sub-Gaussian noise.
items.author: Yuxuan Hou, Yicheng Li

items.title: Community HydroAgent: Formalizing Forecaster Expertise into Skill-Orchestrated Flood Forecasting Workflows
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.23983v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Operational flood forecasting depends on tacit forecaster expertise that is difficult to formalize, audit, and transfer. Although artificial intelligence methods have advanced flood prediction and model-error correction, few studies explicitly represent the tacit expert rules, review checkpoints, and workflow constraints that connect model outputs to operational warning decisions. Here, we propose Community HydroAgent for Flood Forecasting (CHA-Flood), a skill-orchestrated agent framework that embeds Large Language Models (LLMs) into a model-driven flood forecasting workflow, where each skill encodes explicit rules to bound LLM reasoning. We validated its effectiveness using five state-of-the-art LLMs in the South Yamhill River basin (USA). Prior judgment captures observed peak flow and flood volume within 5% tolerance in 10 and 11 out of 14 events, and 5-fold cross-validation over 129 events yields Pearson correlations of 0.62 and 0.84. Building on a high-baseline scheme library (average KGE 0.890), the guided scheme selection further improves KGE by 0.023-0.154. All five tested LLMs successfully execute the CHA-Flood workflow with comparable judgment accuracy (each spanning 40%-80% across cross-validation folds) but with substantial cost differences. Removing only the language-model narrowing lowers median KGE from 0.723-0.753 to 0.662 for all five LLMs, indicating that the gain comes from LLM reasoning rather than from the choice of LLM. CHA-Flood does not aim to replace human forecasters; instead, it translates their tacit expertise into an auditable and reproducible workflow. This skill-orchestrated paradigm demonstrates how explicit rule boundaries can guide LLM reasoning to complement physically based simulation in next-generation flood forecasting.
items.author: Qingyi Yang, Siqian Qiu, Bing Li, Xu Shan, Jia Feng, Shunan Zhou, Xudong Zhou, Tiantian Xing, Jiale Guo, Xiaoyi Dong, Gaoyu Liu, Xiaohuan Liu, Haiqing Pu, Qingwen Deng, Xun Zhang, Zhongrun Xiang, Haiyang Qian, Ying Yan, Yongkang Xu, Nuo Lei, Tianlong Jia, Baoying Shan, Carlo De Michele

items.title: Machine-Learned Compact Subspace Generation for Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction within Density Matrix Embedding Framework
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.20585v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), an extension of quantum selected configuration interaction (QSCI), is a promising hybrid quantum-classical paradigm for molecular ground-state energies. By replacing variational optimization with quantum sampling, QSCI avoids barren plateaus and directly reconstructs correlated wavefunctions. However, existing configuration recovery mainly enforces symmetry constraints without targeting the most physically relevant configurations, often yielding oversized subspaces and costly classical diagonalization. We introduce QSCI-RBM, a compact subspace generation protocol based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), and integrate it within Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET). The RBM learns the distribution of dominant determinants from hardware samples, generating high-probability configurations. Sampling was performed on IBM Heron R1 (\texttt{ibm\_torino}) for CH$_5$NO, R2 (\texttt{ibm\_fez}) for C$_2$H$_4$, and R3 (\texttt{ibm\_boston}) for the larger H$_2$O benchmark and the protein-ligand system. After validating on these benchmarks of increasing active-space size, we simulate the inhibitor Carmofur bound to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (M\textsuperscript{pro}), fragmented into ten DMET impurities. Both DMET-QSCI-RBM and a DMET-SQD baseline reach chemical-potential self-consistency within four $\mu$-iterations. At the converged chemical potential, DMET-QSCI-RBM lies within $0.05\,\mathrm{mHa}$ of DMET-FCI while accessing on average only $0.22\%$ of the symmetry-preserving configuration space, versus $0.55\,\mathrm{mHa}$ at $33.0\%$ for DMET-SQD, leading to a $\sim$153-fold subspace reduction. RBM-assisted expansion thus yields far more compact hardware-derived determinant spaces at equal or better accuracy, reducing classical overhead for scalable quantum embedding of biological systems on real hardware.
items.author: Ashish Kumar Patra, Anurag K. S. V., Ruchika Bhat, Sai Shankar P., Rahul Maitra, Jaiganesh G

items.title: Dynamics-Aware Meta-Imitation for Generalization to Unseen Robotic Manipulation
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.15880v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Imitation Learning aims to learn skills from extensive observations and demonstrations for robots, so it suffers from data scarcity and environment generalization. The existing methods predominantly focus on imitation from in-domain tasks and consequently struggle with generalization to unseen tasks. To bridge this generalization gap, we propose the \textbf{D}ynamics-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{M}eta-\textbf{I}mitation (DAMI) framework. By integrating meta-learning to construct a shared skill space, DAMI equips agents for rapid adaptation to novel tasks. We introduce the Visual-Motor Trajectory (VMT) module to capture complex spatio-temporal dynamics within the task latent space. Furthermore, we propose the Unpaired Unified Task (U2T) block to fuse unstructured multimodal observations. To coordinate these representations, we integrate a Task-Conditioned Feature Modulation (TCFM) mechanism customized for modulating low-level 3D features. By capturing intrinsic dynamics from a random complete reference demonstration, our framework learns the underlying task logic rather than memorizing static cues, ensuring effective generalization. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines regarding direct inference on seen tasks and adaptation to unseen tasks via few-shot fine-tuning.
items.author: Zhenduo Shang, Xiyao Liu, Bohan Li, Xudong Wang, Teng Ren, Lianqing Liu, Zhi Han

items.title: Mixture of Probes: Learning from Privileged Modalities in Multimodal LLMs Through Probing
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.08839v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are typically designed under the assumption that all modalities available during training will also be accessible at inference. However, many real-world settings violate this assumption, requiring models to operate under a privileged modality setting, where auxiliary modalities are available only during training. While these modalities contain valuable information, existing MLLMs largely fail to leverage them effectively, as they treat modalities as interchangeable inputs rather than sources of complementary supervision. We propose Mixture of Probes (MoP), a novel framework that disentangles modality-specific and modality-general signals within the MLLM, allowing the model to preserve modality-dependent structure while learning transferable representations across modalities. At its core, MoP achieves this through a structured probing mechanism that extracts and organizes information from intermediate representations of a shared modality encoder, rather than relying only on final-layer alignment as done in existing MLLMs. To support this disentanglement, we further introduce MoP Cross-modal Training (MoP-X), a training strategy for MoP centered around a probe disentanglement loss that prevents probe collapse and encourages cross-modal learning. We evaluate MoP across two domains spanning eight tasks and four modalities under a comprehensive evaluation protocol tailored to the privileged modality setting, where each modality is independently treated as the sole input at inference time. MoP consistently outperforms strong MLLM baselines, achieving up to 65% relative improvement, demonstrating that auxiliary modalities, even when unavailable at inference, can provide substantial gains when effectively leveraged during training. Code, model checkpoints, and evaluation protocols will be made available at https://github.com/Sony/MoP.
items.author: Dominick Reilly, Qiyu Wu, Hiromi Wakaki, Srijan Das, Yuki Mitsufuji

items.title: Is the Geometry Doing the Work? An Operating-Point Audit of Hierarchy in Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.05268v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models are designed to encode abstraction geometrically: general concepts near the origin, specific ones farther out, and entailment cones representing directed order. We ask whether trained MERU, HyCoCLIP, and PHyCLIP models actually use these mechanisms. We audit seven released checkpoints and matched from-scratch interventions. All audited converged checkpoints remain near-Euclidean in the dimensionless radius $u=\sqrt{c}\rho$: the largest observed image-side value is $0.37$ -- well below $u\approx0.84$, where local metric distortion reaches $10\%$. Releasing the curvature floor changes curvature and norms but not this regime, with mixed, generally modest downstream shifts. Trained entailment cones are saturated or nearly saturated, so low violation rates can arise from trivially wide cones rather than learned order. Preregistered semantic traversal detects weak within-branch order but no operative full-hierarchy readout. Shuffle-controlled tests detect no pair-specific radial ordering in released checkpoints, and no positive result is consistent across all three matched ViT-B seeds. This non-detection is sensitivity-bounded: the diagnostic reaches $80\%$ power only at $\approx13.5$ pp of shuffle-controlled excess, while the largest released gap is $\approx5$ pp. We trace this to a low-curvature shortcut: lowering curvature widens entailment cones and suppresses violations without learning order. In the probed trajectories, gradient decomposition identifies entailment as the dominant curvature-lowering pressure during collapse. Yet curvature contracts even when entailment is removed, so the shortcut is not the sole cause. Under our diagnostics, the audited formulations do not demonstrate an operative radial or cone-based hierarchy. We distill the audit into a five-number geometry report for evaluating future hierarchy claims.
items.author: Jaeyoung Kim, EunSeok Kim, Dongsuk Jang

items.title: Mean Field Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms for Mean Field Control
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.01525v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This monograph provides an introduction to mean field reinforcement learning through the lens of Markov decision processes arising from large-population stochastic control with mean field interactions and common noise. Starting from the connection between multi-agent reinforcement learning and mean field control, it develops the probabilistic, mathematical, and control-theoretic framework needed to formulate representative-agent learning problems, analyze their relationship with finite-population systems, and study both general and linear-quadratic models. The presentation includes dynamic programming principles, propagation-of-chaos limits, and theoretical analyses of tabular Q-learning and policy-gradient methods. It also discusses numerical implementations, including tabular schemes and deep reinforcement learning methods such as deep deterministic policy gradient. The goal is to give readers a coherent bridge between mean field control theory and reinforcement learning methodology, emphasizing the mathematical structure of the problems and the design of tractable learning approaches for large stochastic populations.
items.author: Ren\'e Carmona, Mathieu Lauri\`ere

items.title: AoiZora: Compiler-Agnostic, Placement-Aware Auto-Parallelization for Video Diffusion Transformers
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.17566v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) process tens of thousands of spatio-temporal tokens per denoising step, so low-latency inference and training commonly spread them across several accelerators.
