To capture the distributional mismatch between the DT and real-world environments: the network was trained on imperfect digital-twin data but evaluated on real-world surrobase data. Results show that the proposed method achieves 96.80% top-1 and 98.36% top-3 beam prediction accuracy, while reducing over-the-air sounding overhead by nearly an order of magnitude relative to exhaustive sweeping, outperforming convolutional and deep neural network baselines from prior work.
items.author: Muhammad Kamran Saeed, Ashfaq Khokhar

items.title: VeilFL: Two-Stage Accountability for Anonymous Federated Learning
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01082v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.
items.author: Varesh Mishra, Aysajan Abidin, Bart Preneel

items.title: Adaptive Land Units from Earth Embeddings
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01050v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Modeling land use starts with a choice of spatial units, typically a regular grid of pixels whose resolution is set by the spatial detail the process requires and, often more critically, by the computational budget. With Earth observation data more abundant than ever, we ask whether good land units can instead emerge from the data itself. To do that, we cluster AlphaEarth embeddings with a parallel Bayesian hierarchical clustering into adaptive land units, large where the land is uniform and small where it is highly heterogeneous. Using Denmark as a case study, we turn 402M land pixels into 1.27M newly defined units, about 320 times fewer, without any labels (i.e., unsupervised), making it possible to fit the whole country on a single consumer-grade GPU. Importantly, these units describe the land well, as a regular grid needs about 5 times as many cells to match them against land-use labels, and about 4 times as many against the declared crop of every field. Compared to clustering the satellite images themselves, the embeddings need half the units for the same purity. But more notably, they work as modeling units. Land-use maps learned on them are within a few points of accuracy of pixel models at a small fraction of the cost, and they make whole-country land-use estimates with reliable uncertainty possible in under a minute, where the same model on pixels does not even fit in device memory.
items.author: Albert Alonso, Jamal Jokar Arsanjani, Andres R. Masegosa

items.title: How Close to the Theme? Similarity-Label Conditioning for Game Music Generation
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01047v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Composers develop music from an original idea, controlling how similar each new section is to it, from near repetition to new material. Game music needs this often, as its material repeats over long play. Music models, however, rarely learn to control similarity from real pieces. We further train a pretrained MIDI model on section pairs from Super Mario pieces. A label states each pair's similarity, and a context vector summarises the given section, or context. For 157 test contexts, the model generates six outputs per label. Twelve measures score the outputs; one main measure each covers melody, pitch content, rhythm and note length. On average, outputs requested as similar are more similar to their context than those requested as dissimilar, and not to other pieces. All twelve measures favour them; each main measure stays significant after correction for multiple tests. On melody, the gap comes mainly from more frequent restatement of the context's melody. Against an otherwise identical model without a label, only the request for high similarity makes outputs more similar. In a listening test, ratings followed melodic overlap with the context most closely of all measures.
items.author: Shangxuan Luo, Zixun Guo, Jinjie Shi, Joshua Reiss

items.title: pico-WAM: Evaluating Counterfactual Prediction and Planning Error in a Compact World Action Model
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01039v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: When a World Action Model fails at control, is the bottleneck proposal generation or trajectory scoring? We introduce pico-WAM, a compact model with supplied physical state for tracing policy-dynamics interactions. Using 206 Push-T demonstrations and 15 training seeds, we compare data regimes and search configurations. Counterfactual branch training improves short-horizon cost ranking and enlarges the coverage advantage of policy-restarted over warm-started search by 4.8 percentage points; restart wins under both data regimes. Replacing learned trajectory scores with simulator costs improves coverage by 12.2 points while retaining learned proposals. Substituting simulator states in proposal generation alone shows no detected gain. Component diagnostics and a separate door-opening study show why better ranking need not yield better control or outperform imitation. These controlled interventions identify scoring as an effective improvement target in the tested setting and provide a reproducible protocol for diagnosing compact world models.
items.author: Keivalya Pandya

items.title: Self-Normalized Inference from Riemannian Stochastic Gradient Paths
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01035v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Riemannian stochastic gradient paths estimate constrained parameters, but confidence regions usually require estimating the Hessian and gradient-noise covariance. We develop self-normalized inference from one path by expressing retained iterates in a common random tangent space. Their average and centered partial sums share an unknown covariance factor that cancels in a Brownian bridge pivot. Under suitable regularity conditions, a joint expansion of the averaged estimator and integrated path controls nonlinear coordinate errors using conditional second moments. The procedure uses fixed-dimensional memory and extends to nondegenerate smooth functionals and alternative local coordinates. Numerical studies show competitive coverage relative to plug-in Wald inference while avoiding Hessian and residual-density estimation.
items.author: Xiaotian Chang, Qirui Hu, Yi Liu

items.title: Forecasting Visitor Demand from Open AI-Camera Counts and Weather: Lessons from Japan for Saudi Heritage Sites
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01033v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Small heritage and nature sites need a few days' notice of busy days to plan staff, overflow parking and shuttles, but most have neither sensors nor forecasting expertise. We test what one artificial intelligence (AI) camera counter per site, a public holiday calendar and a free weather forecast can predict. Using 22 months of open AI-camera counts from three contrasting sites in Fukui, Japan (a train station, a coastal cliff and a mountain summit park), we measure how weather changes visits, forecast daily counts up to a week ahead with only the weather forecast available at the time, test busy-day warnings tied to a staffing decision, and ask how much history a new counter needs. The more exposed the site, the more weather matters: 10 mm of rain comes with 3% fewer detections at the station, 9% fewer at the cliff and 37% fewer at the summit park. With the forecasts actually issued, three-day-ahead weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE) at the summit park falls from 38.5% to 31.9% (Diebold-Mariano p<0.001), and the gain holds to five days; the sheltered station gains nothing. Three-day busy-day warnings with forecast weather reach, on past data and under the primary definitions, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.87-0.93, and weather lifts the overflow car park warning's precision from 0.60 to 0.82. For a new counter, blending a learned model with last week's same-hour counts cuts hourly error after only three days of training, pending a real installation. All inputs are off the shelf, and we outline how the approach could apply to heritage sites in Saudi Arabia.
items.author: Amil Khanzada, Mohammed Sohail, Jana Wasfi, Ahmad Showail

items.title: Trouble With Time: Compile Timestamps and First-Seen Date Regression in EMBER2024
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01031v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reliable first-seen dates are important for constructing temporal malware evaluation splits, but this information often comes from external services that are not equally accessible to all researchers. We investigate whether machine learning can instead estimate an executable's first-seen date or determine when its PE/COFF compilation timestamp is unreliable. Using EMBER2024, we evaluate feature-based and raw-byte models across classification, regression, ranking, and latent-reliability formulations. Direct first-seen regression produces errors comparable to a substantial portion of the dataset's collection window, and none of the evaluated scores provides a useful chronological ordering of files. Current models therefore cannot replace externally sourced first-seen metadata. In contrast, classifiers can identify timestamps that fall within specified tolerances of first seen and can detect clearly implausible timestamps with high discrimination. We also find substantial timestamp disagreement among both benign and malicious executables, indicating that unreliable timestamps are not exclusively a product of malicious manipulation. These results establish baselines and identify timestamp reliability as a distinct direction for future security-ML research.
items.author: Edward Raff, Aditya Kapoor

items.title: Robust Pixel-wise Digital Image Correlation under Large Motions and Illumination Variations via a Global-to-Local Hybrid Neural Field
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.01018v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Digital image correlation (DIC) is a widely used non-contact technique for full-field displacement measurement. Data-driven deep-learning DIC offers rapid inference but may generalize poorly to unseen speckle patterns, deformation modes, noise levels, and illumination conditions. Classical optimization-based DIC and recent image-constrained neural formulations avoid labeled displacement data, yet their convergence and accuracy remain vulnerable to initialization, large rigid-body motion, fine non-uniform deformation, and gray-value disturbances. This paper presents a global-to-local hybrid neural DIC framework for robust pixelwise measurement. Stage 1 estimates a dominant in-plane rigid transformation through coarse rotation search, phase correlation, and masked refinement, providing a reliable initialization under large translation and rotation. Stage 2 represents the residual displacement with a hybrid Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP), and optimizes it using a valid-overlap, illumination-robust structural loss. The local gray-value model explicitly accommodates multiplicative and additive intensity changes. Simulated and real experiments demonstrate accurate and stable displacement recovery under noise, non-uniform deformation, large rotation, illumination variation, and degraded imaging conditions.
items.author: Xianglong Guo, Jianyang Li

items.title: HALO: Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00986v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Learning from extensive longitudinal clinical records--spanning repeated encounters, evolving conditions, and heterogeneous documentation--under a finite labeling budget requires solving two coupled problems: deciding what evidence to keep and deciding which patients deserve higher-fidelity labels. Prior work on active learning and multi-fidelity label acquisition mainly addresses the second problem, while treating the evidence presented to the acquisition policy as fixed. We present HALO, a Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning pipeline for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records. This framework jointly learns what to read and what label source to acquire under budget. HALO first selects informative evidence from longitudinal records and then uses a budget-aware policy to allocate free-, silver-, and gold-fidelity label sources. For frozen policies, our theory characterizes asymmetric acquired-label channels and gives a budget-constrained finite-sample gold-risk bound for a common downstream logistic model. In a heart-failure case study, HALO attained the highest MedAlign acquired-label F1 at six of eight target budgets. A downstream classifier trained on HALO-acquired labels attained the highest external MGB F1 at budgets 15-60 and remained within 0.01 of the best comparator at budgets 75-120.
items.author: Huaiyuan Ying, Feiqing Huang, Ryumei Nakada, Katherine P. Liao, Tianxi Cai

items.title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00979v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem.
  We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.
items.author: Gengyu Xue, Fan Wang, Feiyu Jiang, Zifeng Zhao, Yi Yu

items.title: Riemannian Newton Methods with Statistical Inference
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00949v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We develop online statistical inference for Polyak-Ruppert averages of inexact Newton iterates on Riemannian manifolds. A local asymptotic representation separates observation noise, solver randomization, and accumulated implementation bias, and yields one-pass covariance estimators and asymptotically valid Wald regions under local regularity and centering conditions. Independent fresh solves add a positive semidefinite term to the score-sandwich covariance; averaging solver replicas reduces this term in inverse proportion to their number. Slowly varying predictable gains instead cancel from the first order law. Product torus simulations show how Newton scaling shortens an ill-conditioned transient and how retaining solver variation restores coverage. Intrinsic means and principal subspaces provide geometric applications, with a streaming data illustration.
items.author: Xiaotian Chang, Qirui Hu, Yangdi Jiang, Nan Qiao

items.title: Bootstrap Inference for Riemannian Optimization Problems
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00947v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We develop an online multiplier bootstrap for manifold-valued parameters estimated by averaging the iterates of Riemannian stochastic approximation. The method runs weighted iterations alongside the original algorithm, with each path using the same observations while updating its own state and intrinsic average. The weighted averages provide uncertainty assessments without a plug-in asymptotic covariance estimator. Under local stability and regularity conditions, we establish bootstrap consistency and show that a fixed number of paths suffices for asymptotically valid Student intervals and intrinsic confidence regions. The theory accommodates samplewise nonsmooth scores and identifies a critical oracle-bias regime in which the estimator's limiting distribution shifts, but the centered bootstrap distribution does not. Applications include spherical means, positive-definite matrix means and medians, and principal-subspace estimation. Simulations show coverage close to nominal in regular settings, and an analysis of North Atlantic storm locations illustrates descriptive online inference for a spherical center.
items.author: Xiaotian Chang, Qirui Hu, Yangdi Jiang, Nan Qiao

items.title: What Breaks and What Comes Back: Capability Damage and Recovery in Depth-Pruned Small Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00877v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Depth pruning removes whole Transformer blocks to make a language model smaller and faster, but the damage is not spread evenly across what the model can do, and a short fine-tuning run, called healing, decides what comes back. We measure this for small models used as agents. Four instruction-tuned models of 1.2-1.7B parameters (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and OLMo-2-1B) are pruned and healed, and six capabilities are tracked: structured output, function calling, instruction following, mathematical reasoning, safety refusal and knowledge. Three results hold across the families. First, function calling and math collapse in every model (retention 0.00-0.07 of the unpruned score), and the order in which capabilities break agrees closely across the four (Kendall's W = 0.92; 0.62 after correcting for chance floors). Second, which parameters are trained matters as much as which data: fully tuning the last three blocks instead of adding low-rank adapters to all blocks costs up to 0.18 in capped mean retention on three families, and one 300k-token pilot per scope detects this. Third, we test a planner that allocates a 1M-token healing budget from 21 short pilot heals. At a fixed budget it raises the weakest capability on two families, although only one of these gains survives a test that also resamples training seeds. Once its 3.48M pilot tokens are counted, uniform healing with the same total number of training tokens matches or beats every planned variant on every family and retains math significantly better on three of them in an item-level test (on one when seeds are also resampled). Healing longer is a strong and simple baseline that planned recovery must beat. Code, per-item predictions and every result are public.

items.title: Managed Deep Agents v0.10: Browser use and asynchronous subagents
items.summary:
• Browser use: Your agent can book travel or file a claim on sites that have no API. When a site asks you to sign in, the agent hands you the browser window, so your password stays out of the model's messages and traces.
  • Async subagents: A long job can go to a subagent that runs in the background while your agent keeps talking with you. You can ask the agent to check on the job or change its course, and the result comes back to the conversation when the subagent finishes.
  • Thread origins and stopping runs: Replies go back to the Slack thread a request started in, including replies from a scheduled run or from a subagent that finished later. A Stop button in the thread cancels its runs.

‍

Managed Deep Agents v0.10 is out today. It adds browser use, so your agent can work on websites that have no API, and async subagents, which run long tasks in the background while your agent keeps talking to you.

In this post, we cover why agents need each one and how to turn it on, then the rest of the release.

Give your agent a browser

Booking travel, canceling a subscription, or filing a claim all happen on sites built for people clicking through pages, and there's often no API an agent can call. While agents can reason through how to complete the task, they can’t take action on websites without an API. Fetching the page with curl doesn't get far either, it produces HTML before any JavaScript renders the page and the agent can't click anything.

Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse can browse websites to unlock a broader set of use cases, and DataDomesaw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Coding agents need a browser too, to check that a change to an app actually renders and works.

We cover where a browser helps and how it works under the hood in “Browser use in Managed Deep Agents”. To turn it on, declare a browser at your project root:

# browser.py
from managed_deepagents import define_browser

browser = define_browser(scope="thread", idle_ttl_seconds=600)

Managed Deep Agents runs the browser in its own LangSmith sandbox and adds the following browser tools to your agent automatically:

ToolWhat it doesbrowser_snapshotReads the page's accessibility tree and assigns element IDsbrowser_runNavigates and interacts, through JavaScript or batches of actions against snapshot IDsbrowser_screenshotCaptures the page, optionally saving the image to the sandboxbrowser_handoffGives a person control of the window

By default, each conversation gets its own browser, which is reused across turns and starts with no cookies or logins from other threads. With scope="user", each signed-in person gets one browser whose logins carry across all of their conversations, so the agent only asks them to sign in to a site once.

Hand the browser to a person

Most browser agents stop at a login wall or a two-factor prompt. With browser_handoff, the agent hands the window to you instead, so your password never ends up in the model's messages or traces.

The agent calls browser_handoff(reason) and explains why it needs you. Your agent channels — like Slack and Studio — will show have a link to allow users of your agents to hand off browser control natively, which opens a link to interact with the remote browser and a Hand back button . Custom clients can render the handoff artifact themselves. Once you sign in and hand control back, the agent checks the page to see whether the login worked and continues. Handoff returns immediately, so the agent can do other work while it waits. Handoff links expire after 15 minutes.

Handoffs let your agent use a webpage for you, without seeing your credentials.

The browser use docs cover scopes, per-run configuration, and the full handoff flow.

Run subagents in the background

Subagents let an agent hand a focused task to a helper with its own context window. Previously in Managed Deep Agents, subagents ran inline, so the agent called one and waited for its answer. This works for a quick lookup, and still is a supported pattern. But for a long task backed by a synchronous agent, or where multiple agents need to be fanned out, the person talking to the agent waits too, and additional interactions with the orchestrator agent are blocked.

With Managed Deep Agents v0.10, you can run subagents asynchronously, without blocking the orchestrator agent, by adding async to a subagent definition:

from managed_deepagents import define_deep_agent

agent = define_deep_agent(
    name="research-assistant",
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    subagents=[
        {
            "name": "researcher",
            "description": "Researches a topic in the background.",
            "system_prompt": "Research the topic and report your findings.",
            "async": True,
        },
    ],
)

The agent starts an async subagent on its own thread and can keep talking to the user while the subagent(s) run(s). The orchestrator agent starts, checks on, updates, and cancels these tasks with a set of async task tools. Every served agent also gets a background copy of a general-purpose subagent, so it can choose at runtime whether to run delegated work in the foreground or the background.

Async subagents notify the agent on their own, so the agent never sits in a polling loop. What happens next depends on what the agent is doing when a subagent finishes:

When the subagent finishes, the agent isWhat happensBusyIt checks unfinished tasks before each model call, so the result arrives mid-runIdleThe subagent wakes it with a new runPaused on an approvalThe approval is left alone; the result arrives once the user answers

An async subagent shares the agent's sandbox, so it picks up the files the agent already wrote. Its run appears under the agent's run in LangSmith. In Slack, its approvals post back to the original thread, and answering them there resumes the subagent.

Also in v0.10

  • runtime.thread: every thread now carries a record of where it started, such as a Slack thread, and who is on it. Tools can read runtime.thread on any run, which is how a Studio resume, a scheduled run, and an async subagent's wake-up run all reply in the original Slack thread.The runtime docs cover the managed fields tools can read.
  • Stopping runs: Slack threads get a native Stop button that cancels the thread's runs, and Studio can cancel runs on Slack threads.
  • Slack channel handlers (experimental): onEvent decides what each Slack event starts, including mentions, direct messages, other messages, and button clicks. status sets what Slack shows while a run works, and reply: "none"leaves replying to the agent. See the Slack channel docs.
  • Bring your own Slack app: mda deploy asks which app a new Slack channel should use. You can pick one that LangSmith creates and manages, create a new one from a manifest, or use one you already have.
  • resolveUser: when someone messages your agent in a channel like Slack, Managed Deep Agents verifies who sent it. resolveUser maps that sender to the matching user in your own system, so your tools can look up that person's account and permissions. Write it as a function or point it at an endpoint we call, and set it on the identitydeclaration to cover every channel or on a single channel.
  • Breaking changes: connectors.mcp() and the connectors/ layout have been removed. MCP servers must be declared in tools/mcp.ts or tools/mcp.py. The sandbox scope option is also removed. For LANGSMITH_*variables, shell environment variables now win over a project .env.

Getting started

Managed Deep Agents v0.10 is available in public beta today. Start from the docs, or create a new project:

uvx --from managed-deepagents mda init my-agent
cd my-agent
uv run mda deploy

As always, we can't wait for you to tell us what you build.

ICYMI: v0.9 added agent-created schedules, per-run configuration, and Slack reactions. Read the v0.9 post.

items.title: Adaptive-Policy Distillation: Knowledge Injection under Information Asymmetry
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00852v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD), which uses reverse-KL supervision on student rollouts to transfer a context-conditioned model's behavior into student model parameters for closed-book inference, has shown strong results. However, we find that this success does not translate to knowledge injection: across two document-QA benchmarks, OPD injects document knowledge far less efficiently than simple off-policy distillation. We trace this reversal to two failures that are structural, yet sparse across token positions. Reverse KL weights its gradient by the student distribution and therefore barely lifts document-specific tokens the student considers unlikely; after forward KL restores this signal, student rollouts expose later positions on the target trajectory only after generating the preceding tokens correctly, so coverage deteriorates with target length. Motivated by the concentration of teacher-student divergence at these hard positions, we propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose per-token gate jointly shifts the rollout toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL where needed, withdrawing both interventions as the student learns. Without labels or a verifier, APD improves over OPD by up to 54.6%, achieving the best scores of 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 MRR on BioASQ.
items.author: Hojun Cho, Kang Eun Jeon, Jaegul Choo

items.title: Fewer Tokens, More Answers: Verifiable-Reward Tuning of an Ornith-Style VLM for Multi-View Driving QA
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00833v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.
items.author: T N Rickesh, Pranav Vinodh, Sowmya Kamath S

items.title: Answer Correction with Verifiable Rewards: A Gemma-Family Study of Multi-View Driving QA
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00828v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.
items.author: T N Rickesh, Pranav Vinodh, Sowmya Kamath S

items.title: ODC: Orthogonal Drift Correction for Improved Text-to-Image Semantic Alignment at Inference
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00819v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Text-to-image models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality images from textual descriptions. However, they often struggle with "semantic drift," where the generated output fails to precisely align with complex or nuanced text prompts. While recent approaches have attempted to address semantic errors regarding attribute binding or object presence, there remains a gap for a more holistic method that addresses these issues by directly refining the text embeddings of the initial user prompt. In this work, we introduce Orthogonal Drift Correction (ODC), an inference-time guidance method designed to mitigate semantic drift without requiring model retraining or additional user inputs. ODC guides image generation through a two-stage process. In the first stage, it identifies the semantic drift by evaluating the initially generated image against the user prompt in a shared vision-language embedding space. It then isolates the component of this drift vector that is orthogonal to the prompt's direction and translates it back into text via a vocabulary-based surrogate mechanism. In the second stage, it produces refined text conditioning for a second generation pass by feeding both the initial text embedding and the re-embedded drift representation into an adaptive rank-reduced concept removal module. Our experiments demonstrate that ODC consistently improves prompt-image alignment, increasing CLIP scores by up to 5.4% over the baseline on the COALBench-300 and PartiPrompts benchmarks. Furthermore, on the T2I-CompBench complex subset, ODC improves the average 3-in-1 score by 4.5% over the competing methods. As a plug-and-play module, ODC offers a practical and efficient method for improving the reliability of text-to-image models. Code is available at https://github.com/kasrakamali/ODC.
items.author: Kasra Kamali, Basim Azam, Tuan Duong Trinh, Jean Honorio, Naveed Akhtar

items.title: Unbiased Low-Rank Approximation for Repeated Matrix-Vector Multiplication: Stability and Optimal Sampling
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00787v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Replacing the matrix in an iteration with random low-rank matrices can reduce the cost of matrix-vector multiplication. However, even if the sampled matrices equal the original matrix in expectation, the expected squared norm of the random iterates may grow while the original iteration converges. Under a fixed rank bound, we study how to choose the distribution of these random matrices to minimize this growth when sampling independently at each step. We derive an exact formula for the optimal asymptotic growth factor and use it to determine when the expected squared norm can converge to zero. We then characterize precisely when a fixed sampling distribution achieves this optimal factor and construct finite-support optimal distributions in every attainable case. These results determine the minimum rank required for stability and provide optimal sampling designs under the prescribed rank constraint.
items.author: Kang Liu

items.title: Sampling Design and Confidence Tubes for Integral Curves on Riemannian Manifolds
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00771v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We estimate the integral curve of an unknown vector field from noisy tangent vector field on a known compact Riemannian manifold. We consider two sampling settings: independent observations at random locations that have already been collected, and a fixed response budget that allows subsequent locations to be chosen using pilot information. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the passive kernel estimator has curve error of order $n^{-2/(d+3)}$ in probability, with sample size $n$ and manifold dimension $d$. Its functional central limit theorem has a limit characterized by a linear stochastic differential equation. For active sampling, an independent pilot directs one new batch of measurements to neighborhoods of the target curve. Under localization, smoothness and design conditions, this concentration yields expected maximum curve error of order $N^{-1/2}$, including the pilot in the total response budget $N$. Both methods provide simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage under mild conditions. Simulations show narrower active tubes in most reported settings, with improved small-sample coverage in some three-dimensional examples. Ocean-drifter observations illustrate mean-flow reconstruction on the sphere, and a canopy-flow LDA application uses retrospective active sampling to quantify lateral and vertical departures of local mean streamlines.
items.author: Xiaotian Chang, Qirui Hu, Cyrus Mostajeran

items.title: Model-Based Learning of Latent Euclidean Embedding from Relational Data
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00765v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Visualizing and interpreting the dependence structure in relational data often benefits from geometric representations via low-dimensional Euclidean embeddings. However, existing approaches are typically restricted to specific response types, rely on burdensome high-dimensional nonconvex optimization, or lack uniform theoretical guarantees for simultaneous coordinate recovery. To address these limitations, we introduce a unified, distance-based latent space framework for both unipartite and bipartite relational data---accommodating continuous, binary, ordinal, and count-valued observations---via a modular two-stage procedure that decouples signal estimation from geometric recovery. First, we estimate the low-rank signal matrix using spectral denoising. For models with nonlinear link functions, we further apply one-step row- and column-wise refinement to achieve uniform entrywise accuracy. Second, we recover the latent configurations through direct spectral analysis for unipartite data and a low-dimensional alignment optimization for bipartite data. We establish uniform recovery guarantees that characterize the propagation of error from signal estimation to the embedding space. To illustrate the scalability and interpretability of our approach, we apply the proposed method to two real-world datasets: a statistician citation network and European Parliament voting records.
items.author: Yinghang Chen, Yunxiao Chen, Haoran Zhang

items.title: Pricing Today, Shaping Tomorrow: Contextual Dynamic Pricing in Purchase-Driven Evolving Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00719v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Across diverse markets, it is important for firms to balance attracting customers with managing operational conditions, such as workloads and delivery times. Dynamic pricing plays a central role in this tradeoff, as the orders generated today can change the conditions faced by future customers. We develop a novel framework for contextual dynamic pricing with an observed shared state and unknown purchase-driven transitions. The valuation model allows unknown mean functions of customer covariates and state, unknown state-specific scales and a common unknown standardized noise distribution. We propose Shadow-Adjusted Pricing in Evolving Systems (SHAPE), which incorporates a purchase's future revenue consequences into current pricing. Purchase-shadow adjustment and scale standardization reveal a common one-dimensional oracle price map across states, allowing SHAPE to retain its pricing history across value updates without repeating coarse exploration. The same active sales records support price-map learning and joint updates of continuation values and purchase shadows, without fitting the noise distribution or full transition matrices. To support this reuse under purchase-driven feedback, we establish pricing guarantees for history-dependent inputs and stability bounds for the joint updates. Under regularity, coverage and design conditions, we obtain sublinear expected regret against a finite-horizon dynamic oracle for linear, H\"older and sparse linear mean models. For affine valuations at fixed state and feature dimensions, SHAPE matches the static semiparametric minimax time exponent up to logarithmic factors for every fixed noise-tail smoothness order $\beta\ge2$. Numerical experiments further demonstrate the appealing performance of SHAPE.
items.author: Jinjiang Zou, Yang Li, Zemin Zheng

items.title: Adversarial robustness does not entail human-aligned categorization
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00715v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Adversarial training can improve some forms of correspondence between artificial and biological vision, but whether robust classifiers acquire human-aligned classification behavior remains unclear. We generated 1,008 controversial stimuli by optimizing latent inputs to a pretrained GAN to elicit high-confidence disagreements between pairs of robust ImageNet classifiers. We compared four adversarially robust ImageNet classifiers - ResNet-101, ViT-B, ConvNeXt-L, and Swin-L - with two-alternative category judgments from 60 participants. We first evaluated each classifier on stimuli optimized to elicit disagreement with another model. Across classifiers, accuracy in predicting individual participants' single-trial category choices was near chance (48.6-51.3%), whereas majority judgments from other participants predicted responses with 85.0-86.8% accuracy. An analysis incorporating model prediction strength and participants' reported confidence found weak positive model-human correspondence for the two convolutional models. On stimuli optimized for disagreement between other model pairs, all four robust classifiers predicted human responses above chance but less accurately than predictions based on other participants' majority judgments; the same pattern held for 17 additional RobustBench models not used in stimulus generation. Across these 17 models, mean model-participant agreement was 67.3%, versus 81.3% mean participant-participant agreement on the same images. These results identify model-specific failures of human alignment and a model-human mismatch that persists across robust classifiers and substantially exceeds disagreement among human observers. Our findings show that adversarial robustness alone does not guarantee human-aligned categorization and suggest that robustness and human alignment should be evaluated as distinct properties of visual recognition systems.
items.author: Itay Reznik, Raz Lapid, Moshe Sipper, Tal Golan

items.title: Adversarial Robustness Is Not Zero-Day Generalization: A Controlled Evaluation of Flow-Based Intrusion Detectors on Corrected CIC-IDS2017
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00713v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Synthetic variants of known attacks, including feature-space adversarial perturbations, are sometimes used as stand-ins for unseen ("zero-day") attacks when evaluating machine-learning network intrusion detection systems (NIDS). We test whether this proxy holds. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 release we train Random Forest, XGBoost, a 1D-CNN and an FT-Transformer and compare, at a fixed 1% false-positive rate over five seeds, detection under constrained perturbations of known attacks (gradient-based and black-box attacks on 42 attacker-controllable features) with leave-one-attack-family-out (LOAO) detection, where an entire family is absent from training. Detection under the strongest perturbation we tested, with budgets of at most 0.2, stays between 90.9% and 99.7%, yet mean detection of held-out families falls to 76.2% (RF), 40.2% (XGBoost), 25.8% (1D-CNN) and 22.8% (FT-Transformer). Robustness exceeds LOAO detection for every model (gaps of 24 to 72 percentage points, 23 to 66 when robustness is also averaged over families; Holm-adjusted p $\le$ 0.00096), and the two measures agree at most on a coarse ranking of the models. An exact mixed-integer evasion search confirms the tree ensembles' scores. Benign-only anomaly detectors and a simple multi-class open-set baseline do not close the gap. A temporal split on 5 seeds (3 of the 4 models) leaves the gap in place. On CSE-CIC-IDS2018 the gap recurs for every model (16 to 68 points). On these benchmarks and under this threat model, a robustness score should not be read as a zero-day score, and the two should be reported separately. Code and per-seed results are publicly available.
items.author: Abdulhamid Zaro

items.title: Personalized Rollout Allocation for Federated LQR Policy Optimization under Heterogeneous Process Noise
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00712v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study federated model-free learning of a common linear quadratic regulator (LQR) gain under a limited uplink communication budget, with clients that share dynamics and costs but experience different process-noise levels. Conventionally, clients transmit gradient matrices whose dimension equals the number of controller parameters. Exploiting the structure of two-point zeroth-order estimates, we consider an implementation in which clients transmit only one scalar cost-difference coefficient per rollout pair, while the server regenerates the associated perturbation directions from shared seeds. Communication thus scales with the number of rollout pairs rather than the controller dimension, turning the uplink budget into a rollout budget. Because noise heterogeneity produces gradient estimates of widely differing variance and every client carries equal weight in the fleet objective, uniform rollout allocation allows noisy clients to dominate the aggregated update and increases the probability of destabilizing updates. We propose a rollout-allocation scheme that assigns rollout pairs in proportion to the standard deviation of each client's estimates and show that it minimizes the variance of the aggregated update. The scheme is implemented exactly through a greedy integer allocation rule whose weights are estimated from the communicated scalars. We further prove that a single allocation factor quantifies its improvement over uniform allocation in a one-round instability bound, the certified step size, and the error floor of a joint stability and convergence guarantee. Simulations show that, under the same communication budget, personalized allocation reduces the one-step instability rate from $37\%$ to $0.3\%$.
items.author: Mohammadreza Rostami, Shahriar Talebi, Solmaz S. Kia

items.title: Boosted Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Homogeneous and Non-Homogeneous Lane-Emden Type Equations
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.00701v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The Lane-Emden Equation is a class of nonlinear differential equations commonly used to model phenomena in astrophysics and mathematical physics, such as stellar structure and thermal behavior in polytropic gas spheres. This study presents a novel hybrid framework that integrates Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) with boosting methods to enhance the accuracy and robustness of solutions for Lane-Emden type differential equations. Standard PINNs leverage physical laws encoded within the loss function, but their predictive performance can be constrained by optimization challenges and approximation errors. To address this, we introduce a post-processing boosting stage where the residual errors from the PINN prediction are modeled using some regression algorithms - including LightGBM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Regression (SVR). The outputs from these boosted models are aggregated to generate a corrected, high-fidelity prediction. The proposed methodology is systematically validated through quantitative metrics and comparative analysis against the standard PINN baseline. The results demonstrate that the boosted PINN framework significantly reduces prediction error, and improves generalization, offering a powerful and flexible approach for solving scientific and engineering problems governed by differential equations.
items.author: Luke Oluwaseye Joel

items.title: Your Agent Just Paid for Nothing: 6 Attacks on x402 Payments - Ishween Kaur, SoFi
items.summary:
x402 lets AI agents pay for data and APIs with tiny on-chain payments over HTTP. Ishween Kaur explains how the protocol works, then walks through six of the 20 ways she broke it in a safe test environment: price changes in the payment header, paying twice, getting data for free, one payment unlocking many pages, lookalike sellers, and prompt injection that talks an agent into paying again. For each one, she shows the guard that stopped it and how to roll out agent payments safely, trace by trace.

Vals AI builds benchmarks that frontier labs cite in their model cards, and Rayan Krishnan explains why those single scores hide a jagged frontier. items.title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
items.summary:
Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests). Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production. Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details [...]

Read More...

The post Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests).
  • Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production.
  • Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests.

Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale.

Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests. More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests), a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch.

In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives.

The Advantage of Catching JiTTests

Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not.

How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta

JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives).

It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers?

To address this, we developed two tandem workflows:

  • An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points.
  • A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”).

To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives.

We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch.

How It Works

The entire system workflow happens in five stages:

Stage 1: Targeting and Triggering 

The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism similar to Diff Risk Score (DRS) and trained on previous code changes. This helps ensure test generation is focused on diffs that are most likely to contain severe regressions.

Stage 2: Two Diff-Aware Test-Generation Workflows

The dodgy diff workflow treats each diff as if it were a mutant and uses mutation-guided LLM-based test generation to produce tests that distinguish the diff’s behavior from its parent. The goal here is to maximize the pool of weak catches and with it the chances of finding a strong catch among them.

At the same time, the intent-aware workflow uses an LLM to infer the diff’s intention using the code changes, diff title, and summary. The LLM then describes the “risks”— the ways an attempt to implement the intent could produce errors. It then uses those risk descriptions to construct mutants — each representing a bug that could be introduced while implementing the inferred intent.

Tests are generated to kill each mutant (i.e., distinguish mutant behavior from parent).

Those tests are then run on the actual diff. Any that fail are harvested as weak catches.

Stage 3: LLM-as-Judge Ensemble (Automated Assessment)

Once weak catches are generated, the system must determine whether each is a false positive or actually a strong catch (true positive).

The LLM-as-Judge ensemble consists of a collection of LLMs that review:

  • The weak-catch test-case code.
  • The test-execution outcome (failure code, message, execution trace).
  • The code changes between parent and child (the diff).
  • The inferred diff intent.

Stage 4: Rule-Based Assessor (RubFake)

We complement LLM-as-Judge with a more traditional, rule-based approach called Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment (RubFake).

LLM-as-Judge has rich semantics, but its judgements are non-deterministic and challenging to verify. By contrast, RubFake provides verified, deterministic judgments. Working together, RubFake and LLM-as-Judge produce an overall ranking of weak-catch candidates, with those ranked sufficiently highly being worthy of further consideration.

Stage 5: Human-on-the-Loop (Engineer Reach-Out)

Based on the ranking from LLM-as-Judge and RubFake, the system then decides whether to reach out to human engineers.

Rather than a human-in-the-loop approach, where a human engineer reviews every output, we’ve reduced friction through a human-on-the-loop approach, where human engineers set criteria and review outcomes at an aggregate level rather than supervising every output.

The Impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta

With the testing system in place, our goal is to get engineers to engage with its results.

As of this writing, 589 engineers at Meta (64% of our outreach) have engaged with Catching JiTTests. These engineers have reported that Catching JiTTests surfaces genuinely actionable findings, with a 60% rate of true positives.

In the first half of 2026, Catching JiTTests played a key role in catching 74 serious (SEV) privacy bugs at the diff stage, before they landed in production and lowering the overall occurrence of privacy SEVs by 20% during that timeframe.

Why It Matters

Agentic software development is helping engineers and developers across the industry write, review, and ship code faster than ever before. But faster deployment means there’s also a need for faster testing. Every bug caught before it reaches production is one that end users never need to deal with. We’ve shown that LLMs can provide an additional safety layer capable of catching what traditional tests may miss, demonstrating that AI-generated testing can scale enough to reduce organizational risk. 

Catching JiTTests is a solution that is scalable, both technologically and socially. Combining these tests with a human-on-the-loop approach helps ensure that engineers rarely need to read test code and only need to confirm whether an observed behavioral change was intended.

The approach is generalizable: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level, and intervene at the policy level rather than per item.

Read the Paper

Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” which was presented at FSE 2026 and featured at Product@Scale, details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests in Meta’s infrastructure.

The post Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: Browser Use in Managed Deep Agents
items.summary:
• A browser lets agents do work on the web that APIs can't cover, including clicking, scrolling, and filling out forms.
  • Managed Deep Agents now runs a browser for your agent, with tools tuned for context-efficient browser use.
  • Managed Deep Agents ships with support for thread and user scoped browser sessions. Handoffs allow users to log into and interact with websites with credentials persisted across sessions.

Agents have gotten good enough to work where we work, and a lot of that work happens in a browser. Booking travel, canceling a subscription, or filing a claim all happen on sites built for people clicking through pages, including ones the agent didn't plan to visit. Often there's no API an agent can call. Fetching the page with curl doesn't get far either, since it returns the HTML before any JavaScript renders the page and can't click anything.

Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse already work this way. Browser agent traffic is growing fast too, and DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone.

Managed Deep Agents lets you build and deploy agents in LangSmith without running any infrastructure. You write the agent's instructions and tools, and LangSmith runs the harness and runtime. Today, we're giving these agents a browser, so you can build your own agents that work on the web. Managed Deep Agents runs the browser too, and gives your agent tools tuned for it.

In this post, we cover where a browser helps and how to turn it on, including handing the browser to a person when the agent needs one. Then we walk through how it works under the hood. Agents built with open source Deep Agents can use a browser too. We'll cover how we tested and tuned the browser tools in a deep dive next week.

Where a browser helps

With a browser and tools to drive it, an agent can read what renders on a page and click through it, the same way you (a human) would.

So far, two common use cases have emerged:

  • Actions an API can't cover, like booking a flight or a restaurant reservation. When a site does have an API for the task, the agent should use the API.
  • End-to-end testing, like checking a frontend change before it merges. When a pull request changes a signup form, a coding agent can start the app in its sandbox, open the form in a browser, and click through it to check that the change works. We use this in Open SWE, our coding agent.

Adding browser use capabilities

To add a browser, export a browser from browser.py at the project root:

# browser.py
from managed_deepagents import define_browser

browser = define_browser(
    scope="thread",
    idle_ttl_seconds=600,
)

scope controls how browser sessions are shared.

  • scope="thread" (the default) gives each thread its own browser. Every conversation starts with a fresh browser window, with no cookies or logins left over from another thread.
  • scope="user" shares one browser across a signed-in user's threads (see Identity). Each thread gets its own window, so two conversations running at once don't click over each other, but they share cookies and other browser state. If you sign in to a site in one thread, a later thread can pick up that session instead of starting over.

The browser stops after idle_ttl_seconds without activity (10 minutes by default), so you don't pay for a browser nobody is using.

Hand off the browser to a user

Some steps still need a person, and signing in is the most common one. You don't want to give the agent your password, where it would end up in the model's messages, in traces, and with a model provider.

So when the agent hits a login page, it calls browser_handoff with a reason, like "Please sign in to Acme Travel so I can continue." In LangSmith Studio, the UI where you chat with and debug your agent, you get an interactive card with the same browser. You sign in yourself, click Hand back, and the agent picks up where it left off, already signed in. Handoff comes with every managed browser and works automatically in Managed Deep Agents channels like Slack, so there's nothing extra to set up.

This matters most with scope="user". With user scope, the sign-in carries over to your later threads, so the agent asks you to log in once, the same way your own browser remembers you.

How it works under the hood

An agent needs two things to use the web: a browser, and a toolset to drive it. Managed Deep Agents manages both.

The browser. Managed Deep Agents runs the browser in its own LangSmith sandbox, separate from the agent. It's a remote browser, so nothing runs on your machine. Unlike most remote browsers, it also has a private link to the agent's sandbox, which is what makes end-to-end testing work (more below).

The tools. Managed Deep Agents adds the browser tools to the agent:

  • browser_snapshot reads the page's accessibility tree and labels interactive elements with IDs.
  • browser_run acts on the page, either with a batch of actions like click and fill or with JavaScript that uses a Playwright-style page object, which Stagehand translates into its own commands.
  • browser_screenshot captures the rendered page.
  • browser_handoff passes the browser to a person, who hands it back when they're done (see above).

browser_run does most of the work. It takes code, so the agent can write a whole chain of steps (open a page, fill a field, click, check the result) as one call and return only what it needs. That keeps long browser tasks fast, and it keeps most of the page out of the agent's context.

The tools are built on Stagehand, Browserbase's open source SDK for building browser agents. We tested and tuned them with the agent development lifecycle: running browser benchmarks, reading the traces in LangSmith, and validating each change with evals. On 100 tasks from WebVoyager, a benchmark of everyday tasks on live websites, they passed 90% of tasks for $1.98 in total. That was the highest pass rate of the seven toolsets we tested. The closest, Browserbase's MCP server, passed 89% at 9x the cost.

This setup supports both use cases, in slightly different ways.

Actions an API can't cover

For tasks like booking a reservation, the agent only needs the browser. Its browser tools send commands to the browser sandbox, which drives the page.

End-to-end testing

End-to-end testing needs one more piece. The app under test runs in the agent's own sandbox, so the browser has to reach it. Two connections make that work:

  • The agent controls the browser through its browser tools, as above.
  • The browser reaches the app through a localhost bridge. When the browser opens localhost:5173, the request travels over a private link to port 5173 in the agent sandbox. The app doesn't need a public URL. Here, localhost means the agent's sandbox.

The agent starts the app with execute, opens it in the browser, clicks through real flows like a signup form, and checks what renders.

Once a test passes, you can ask the agent to save its steps as a test file, since each browser_run call is a piece of an ordinary Playwright script. Later runs replay that file with no model calls until the page changes.

Conclusion

Browsers open up a huge part of the web to agents, from booking a flight to testing the app a coding agent just built. With Managed Deep Agents, giving your agent a browser takes a few lines of code, and the tools behind it are tuned to be fast and context-efficient.

Add a browser to a managed agent with define_browser. To give an open source deep agent a browser, where you bring your own (like a hosted one from Browserbase), see the browser use guide.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Sean McGuire, Miguel Gonzalez, and Kyle Jeong from Browserbase for their help with Stagehand and this post.

items.title: From PID to Reinforcement Learning in Building HVAC Control: A Control-Architecture Review of Tuning Strategies, Formulations, and Deployment Trade-offs
items.summary: This paper reviews control architectures for building heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, addressing the tension among energy demand, occupant comfort and equipment operability, and situating proportional-integral-derivative (PID) regulation within a layered control stack that also includes rule-based and model-based supervisory control and data-driven reinforcement learning (RL). It examines the thermostat-PID layer from two-position and scheduled setpoint control through proportional, PI and PID regulation and their tuning, then formulates RL for building control as a Markov decision process. Its central contribution is a taxonomy of where RL meets PID: RL as a gain tuner for an existing loop, as a direct replacement for the regulatory controller, as a hybrid with model predictive control, and as supervisory setpoint and schedule generation. Across these classes, the review establishes that the physical loop remains invariant while the intervention point changes, and that the classes differ in their requirements for actuation authority, state information, modelling, commissioning and constraint handling. It further establishes that PID is inexpensive and well codified but limited by nonlinearity, time variation, discrete mode switching, loop interaction and slow plant dynamics, while RL's admissible position must be argued rather than assumed. The paper concludes that these architectures are not competing philosophies of control but nested points of attachment on one HVAC plant, with hybrid implementations possible, and that deployment trade-offs must be assessed according to the specific control interface and scaffolding required.
items.author: Armin Keshavarz

items.title: FlowBatt: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Battery Degradation Prediction
items.summary: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.
items.author: Steffen Blömeke

items.title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
items.summary: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.
items.author: Andreas Krause

items.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
items.summary: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.
items.author: Junchi Yan

items.title: Meet Students Where They Are: Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation for On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates the student's exposure bias by optimizing on student-generated trajectories. However, student-generated prefixes may contain reasoning errors or follow patterns unfamiliar to the teacher, undermining the reliability of its token-level supervision. This degradation becomes more pronounced as prefixes grow longer. To address this teacher-side distribution mismatch, we propose Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA), which adapts the teacher to the states on which it is queried during distillation. Specifically, before OPD starts, we collect student rollout prefixes with random lengths and continually train the teacher to continue from the prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). By treating each prefix as context and rewarding correct final answers, the teacher learns to recover from student-induced states rather than imitate the student's reasoning. Then, the adapted teacher is used for standard OPD, with no changes to the distillation objective. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our SPTA improves average student performance over standard OPD and OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers. These results highlight the importance of adapting teachers not only to solve problems independently, but also to provide reliable guidance on the states their students actually visit.
items.author: Jinan Xu

items.title: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements
items.summary: Despite recent advances in CUAs, their development remains constrained by the limited diversity, controllability, and reliability of interaction data. Moreover, conventional optimization pipelines lack iterative feedback, while existing recursive improvement approaches often rely on self-generated experiences, limiting ability expansion and yielding diminishing returns. To address these challenges, we introduce CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive improvement framework. At the system level, an outer world-data-model flywheel continuously incorporates open-world corpus and leverages evolving model weaknesses to guide subsequent data construction and optimization iterations. At the data level, an inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation. The former mines authentic workflows as seed tasks from instructional videos, and employs visual-semantic dual-path trajectory reconstruction; The latter transforms these seeds into reusable primitives for controllable synthesis of diverse, complex, and verifiable tasks. To enable efficient and reliable trajectory collection, we further introduce a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism in various real environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUA-Master-27B achieves competitive performance across GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks, scoring 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench, and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam. Our framework also substantially improves the quality and efficiency of data synthesis, and exhibits continuous gains across recursive iterations.
items.author: Xiangyu Yue

items.title: Inner optimizers in active-learning Kriging reliability analysis: a pre-specified comparison and the unconservative estimates left by unlearned failure modes
items.summary: Active-learning Kriging often replaces candidate pools by continuous metaheuristic search. A pre-specified comparison sharing surrogate, population and stopping rule isolated this inner optimizer: five budget-matched continuous optimizers, including hybrid swarm optimization with L-BFGS-B polishing, against candidate pools on eleven problems (dimension 2 to 100). The primary hypothesis was not supported: against optimizers sharing its criterion the hybrid won 6, tied 41 and lost 19 of 66 Holm-corrected accuracy comparisons, and against pool methods 0, 23 and 21 of 44. With sequential selection on three series systems, multistart L-BFGS-B left a failure mode unlearned in 59 of 60 runs, more often than swarm, genetic-algorithm or AK-MCS. In all 198 runs (22 post-freeze) with an unlearned mode, the learned modes did not compensate and failure probability was underestimated (exploratory). The error criterion can accept substantial underestimation: it accepted 17 runs (13 pool-selected) at 0.38 to 0.89 of the reference; 181 exhausted the budget. Follow-up analyses on single-design-point problems indicate underestimation when selections concentrate near the design point. Kriging-believer pool selection satisfied the surrogate stopping criterion with fewer calls than the best continuous method in all four informative batch cells (two post-freeze). We recommend default pool selection and coverage checks for any selection.
items.author: Wei-Chang Yeh

items.title: Preprocessing Choices in Fine-Tuning Data Matter: Utility and Demographic Sensitivity in LLM-Based Recommendation
