To support this transition, this paper introduces PR4Code, a dataset of 4,508 Java and 8,831 Python curated Pull Requests (PRs) collected from GitHub, each enriched with metadata, commit histories, and detailed code changes. Unlike resources focused on isolated code fragments, PR4Code captures the feature implementation process, delivering a large and diverse collection of real-world development tasks that can be used to assess AI-driven solutions. Our analysis reveals substantial variability in PR structure, commit granularity, and textual content. In addition, we release scripts to regenerate and update the dataset, ensuring reproducibility and maintainability.
items.author: Benedetta Donato, Leonardo Mariani, Daniela Micucci, Oliviero Riganelli

items.title: STORY2DIFF: A Dataset Linking Real-World User Stories to Code Changes
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39872v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Research on requirements-to-code tasks needs examples in which a genuine requirement is paired with the change that implemented it. Existing user-story collections, however, largely contain isolated or synthetic text. To address this limitation, we present STORY2DIFF, a dataset of 7,785 English user stories linked to merged pull requests from January 2017 to July 2026. The dataset is mined from a set of 982 public Java and Python repositories. Each record in the dataset combines the original issue, extracted Connextra elements, the associated pull request and commit metadata, a file-level diff capturing the code changes introduced by the associated pull request, and the affected files before and after the change. The tool we built to mine STORY2DIFF can be used to repeat the automatic extraction of the records, using different parameters (e.g., a different timeframe). The dataset can support a variety of tasks, including requirement discovery, traceability, change- impact estimation, and requirements-aware code generation. Dataset: https://github.com/riganelli/user-story-mining-pipeline/ releases/tag/V4.0.1. Video: https://youtu.be/qOhXUeyeiTQ.
items.author: Benedetta Donato, Daniele Franchini, Alessandro Greco, Oliviero Riganelli, Daniela Micucci, Leonardo Mariani

items.title: Early Prediction of Cross-Service Implementation Scope: Evidence and Limits from Multiple Microservice Projects
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Microservice architectures aim to localize change, yet feature requests may require implementation across service boundaries. We investigate how well such downstream scope can be anticipated before implementation begins. Using issue--pull-request--commit traceability and implementation evidence corrected through targeted human adjudication, we reconstruct 866 repository-traceable feature requests from 13 open-source microservice projects and map their implementations to validated service boundaries. Cross-service changes occur in 101 requests (11.7%) and exhibit broader implementation footprints, particularly higher code churn, but no clear difference in lead time. Pre-implementation evidence provides limited cross-project predictive signal: the strongest leave-one-system-out model reaches a project-macro Macro-F1 of 0.484, but its advantage over the majority baseline is not significant after Holm correction and is sensitive to small evaluation folds. A local LLM offers no reliable improvement over classical models. Downstream workload is substantially harder to estimate, as learned models do not consistently outperform training-fold median baselines. A simple service-mention heuristic also performs comparably to learned scope triage. These findings show that early feature-request evidence is more useful for lightweight cross-service scope triage than for automated scope determination or precise workload estimation.
items.author: Zhoumaocuo, Xiaozhou Li

items.title: When Static Reachability Says No: Checking Joern-Based Negative Verdicts for Python Against Execution
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39504v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A negative reachability verdict removes a finding from human review. We check such verdicts against execution. Our pipeline, SourceLens, maps Semgrep findings to a Python program's call graph, whose edges a query takes from the calls that Joern links in its code property graph. We ran two command-line programs from the PyCG macro-benchmark, in which the benchmark's manual call graph and Joern disagree, under coverage and recorded the calls between their functions. On these edges, 123 functions of asciinema are unreachable from the program's entry points. The project's own integration script executes 86 of them, and all our runs 113. In Sublist3r, 19 of 24 are executed. The latest Joern release gives the same verdicts. The missing calls go through values, such as classes and functions passed around, or have no call expression, as in with blocks and property reads. In asciinema, four missing edges make 50 of the 113 executed functions reachable. The manual call graphs also lack observed calls, in asciinema many of them property reads and with blocks, which the benchmark may not count as calls. A rule that turns negative verdicts into unknown recovers 62 of the 113 and 15 of the 19, mostly through dunder and private method names. It recovers 0 of the 5 security findings with a negative verdict, all in executed functions. Its selectivity cannot be measured, as only 10 and 5 negative verdicts were not executed, and under library entry-point models it degrades every negative verdict.
items.author: Artur Zi\k{e}ba-Kozarzewski, Bartosz Grzegorzewski

items.title: Program Bindings Inside Code Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39489v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Code language models complete, review, and repair programs without exposing the program structure encoded in their hidden states. In this paper, we test whether the hidden states of a code model can be described and edited using the information a compiler front end computes. For each token of a Python program, standard analyzers provide its position in the abstract syntax tree, its scope, its definition-use links, and its syntactic category. We fit a decomposition that expresses every hidden state of a frozen model as a sum of one term per token, each combining the token with this structural label, and we replace the model's own states with the decomposition at every layer while it predicts the output of a small program. If the model still answers correctly, the decomposition preserves the information the model uses. We apply this test to 14 open models, seven of them trained for code, and compare against a baseline decomposition of the same size built from token positions. The static-analysis decomposition preserves the model's answers better than the positional one in 10 of the 14 models, including six of the seven code models, and deleting the definition-use links from it removes most of that advantage on the two models tested. Editing the decomposition, for instance rebinding the argument of a call, makes StarCoder2-15B produce the answer of the edited program in 90 of 100 cases, compared with 19 for the positional baseline. The Qwen2.5 family is the exception on several measures. For most of the models tested, standard static analysis therefore provides both a description of what the hidden states encode about a program and a way to change it without retraining.
items.author: Prateek Kumar Rajput, Yewei Song, Jacques Klein, Tegawend\'e F. Bissyand\'e

items.title: QSoftCore: A Conceptual Foundation for Quantum Software Engineering
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39406v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum software engineering (QSE) requires understanding application requirements, quantum programs and algorithms, quantum computation paradigms, executions, and deployment. However, relevant quantum computing (QC) concepts are often defined across physical, mathematical, and paradigm-specific levels of abstraction, making it difficult for the QSE community and hence proposed methods to refer to them consistently. To this end, we present QSoftCore, a conceptual model that reorganizes established QC concepts from a software engineering perspective and connects quantum applications, computational problems, algorithms, configurations, programs, and paradigm-specific computation specifications with state evolution, execution results, and backends. Our assessment against QSE literature across key software engineering activities indicates that QSoftCore provides shared QC referents for quantum computations, executions, deployment configurations, backends, and measurement evidence across the QSE lifecycle.
items.author: Tao Yue, Yuechen Li, Man Zhang

items.title: Omission-Safe Conditional Contracts for Evidence-Closed CI Qualification
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continuous-integration evidence is conditional: a workflow determines which jobs should run, while an archive records which jobs remain observable. Reconstructing requirements from those observations lets an omission erase its own obligation. We present a qualification method that compiles a pinned workflow into conditional job requirements independently of target presence, retains a fixed capture inventory, and checks source-complete derivation certificates with a separate implementation. For a fixed source, context, scope and binding universe, with sound obligations and applicability judgments that preserve established truth under information extension, withdrawing observation facts cannot create authorization. The implementation handles static matrices, dependency guards and bounded pinned reusable workflows, preserving unknown applicability and separating tolerated outcomes from evidence coverage. Both implementations match the 45 hand-specified authorization controls, reject 180 source-certificate attacks, and exhibit no authorization gain over 704 distinct proper development erasures. An explicitly witnessed 12-job platform run qualifies in both implementations; all 4,095 proper payload-subset erasures block authorization. A frozen collection spans 240 runs in eight workflow families across six projects. All 160 evaluation source certificates independently validate, but unavailable historical execution-source identities leave actual qualification open. Initial gate diagnoses agree on 155/160 runs; a preserved unknown-propagation repair yields 160/160 agreement in a retrospective rerun. The study establishes bounded source extraction and omission resistance, rather than natural-fault prevalence or producer authenticity.
items.author: Zhiheng Zhang

items.title: PyReprism: A Shared Lexical Foundation for Polyglot Code Analysis
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39224v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Empirical studies of polyglot repositories apply the same analyses to every language of a corpus, such as separating code from comments, computing metrics, normalizing identifiers, and screening for duplicated code. Assembling them from specialized tools introduces differences in language coverage, measurement conventions, and workflows. We present PYREPRISM, an open-source Python library and command-line tool that separates language-specific lexical processing from reusable analyses: each language declares its lexical surface, which yields a lossless stream of typed tokens, and every analysis is implemented once on that stream. Across 187 built-in languages, language-specific declarations have a median length of 16 lines, and no language overrides a shared analysis. Against a reference parser, comment and string classification reach F1 scores of 0.994 and 0.958 on 1,412 files in 12 languages that were never used to develop the tokenizer. In a study of a polyglot repository, one tool replaces three; with matched inputs and analysis operations, it takes 2.9s instead of 8.7s on one core. We also characterize where lexical analysis falls short, in complexity estimation and clone screening. Tool: https://github.com/unlv-evol/PyReprism Video: https://youtu.be/IXc-NP5t4GU
items.author: Daniel Ogenrwot, Jorge Gonzalo Delgado Cervantes, Richard Sserunjogi, John Businge

items.title: Do Open-Source Video Ad Clients Follow VAST 4.3? An Empirical Study of Player Conformance
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.39093v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Context. Video ads reach streaming and connected-TV apps through VAST documents, and companies count ads from the HTTP requests the player's client library sends. A tracking error can leave playback intact and surface later as disagreeing counts.
  Objective. To measure how far open-source VAST clients meet the player duties of VAST 4.3, whether verdicts depend on the runtime, what generated inputs add, and when deviations were introduced.
  Method. A catalog of 108 requirements was extracted from the specification. Six open-source clients in eight configurations ran against 69 crafted test vectors and the IAB's sample tags, under Node.js and in five browsers on three engines, with every request recorded. Grids, fuzzing and a sweep over 36 releases extend the catalog; Google's closed IMA SDK is a comparison.
  Results. The open-source clients have 78 findings and 3 to 21 must-level deviations per configuration. None of the tested open-source clients that follow redirect (Wrapper) chains fills the required macros in a Wrapper's request; the archived IMA 3.794.0 configuration tested does. One library's timeout throws an exception no caller can catch, ending a Node.js process. In a pod (ads played back to back), one player credits a finishing ad's completion to the next ad, fixed in release 5.3.0. A library can conform under jsdom and deviate in every tested Chrome- and Safari-family browser.
  Conclusions. The tested clients diverge on the duties other companies use to count and diagnose ads. A shared conformance suite run in real browsers could expose most graded deviations; the harness and vectors are released.
items.author: Prashant Chaudhary

items.title: When Relevant Code Is Wrong: Runtime-Aware Context for AI Coding Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38800v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI coding agents increasingly rely on retrieved code and development history to guide software changes. However, highly relevant artifacts may describe implementations that are inactive or incompatible with the target deployment. Neither semantic similarity nor recency establishes whether retrieved information remains applicable under feature flags, architectural migrations, and deployment-specific configurations. We challenge relevance-oriented retrieval by introducing operational context validity, a task-, deployment-, and time-dependent criterion for determining whether software evidence can legitimately guide implementation decisions. We instantiate this new retrieval principle in CASE, an agent-agnostic framework that connects repository artifacts with runtime configurations and architectural evolution, classifies evidence as valid, invalid, or unknown, and generates context packages distinguishing actionable guidance from historical rationale and unresolved constraints. We investigate its feasibility through a reproducible preliminary evaluation involving six development tasks, 15 artifacts, and three deployments. Conventional retrieval exposes 16 incompatible artifact occurrences as actionable, whereas CASE excludes them while retaining all applicable artifacts under the prototype's reference rules. Recency filtering reduces valid recall to 0.43, while removing feature-flag evidence from CASE reduces it to 0.13. Although these results demonstrate feasibility rather than improvements in coding-agent correctness, they reveal limitations of relevance-based retrieval and motivate a new research direction: enabling coding agents to reason not only about which information is relevant, but also whether it remains operationally valid.
items.author: Wesley K. G. Assun\c{c}\~ao, Ramesh Periyathambi

items.title: Write Once, Instrument Anywhere: Portable, Sandboxed Tooling with WebAssembly Components
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monitoring and debugging deployed software is crucial for scalability, performance, and robustness. Cross-cutting concerns are pervasive across software ecosystems, yet engineers must address them with a fragmented toolbox. While high-level frameworks exist to offer application-level types and semantics, they often lock a solution into specific languages, runtimes, or hardware architectures. Portability often forces engineers to choose lower-level instrumentation mechanisms. For example, in-language frameworks can trace a request across processes, but multi-language contexts require instrumentation at the boundary, for example using eBPF. While these frameworks provide powerful capabilities, they often result in 1) a tradeoff between application-level types or low-level bytes and packets, 2) non-composable domain-specific tools, 3) feature fragmentation across frameworks, and 4) tools that often run with unrestricted access to the program and its environment.
  We address these problems with Splicer, a WebAssembly component interposition framework that 1) provides semantically rich application-level types, 2) enables pluggable tooling with powerful capabilities, 3) reduces ecosystem fragmentation through porting across languages and hardware, and 4) confines each tool to a sandbox with explicitly granted permissions. We evaluate Splicer on a suite of benchmarks demonstrating the pluggability of non-trivial tooling written in multiple source languages and their performance.
items.author: Elizabeth Gilbert, Chris Fallin, Heather Miller, Ben L. Titzer

items.title: The Reality Gap in Automated Driving Systems Testing: Landscape, Challenges, and Research Directions
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38628v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Simulation is essential for testing automated driving systems (ADS), but discrepancies between simulation and reality can undermine testing conclusions. It remains unclear which discrepancies the literature addresses and what evidence supports correspondence claims. We present a systematic mapping of 235 primary studies that measure or mitigate the reality gap in ADS testing, selected from 4,195 publications. We characterise objectives, targets, approaches, experimental setups, and evaluation evidence. Our classification distinguishes simulated and real-world execution across six ADS test components, separately for each approach and its evaluation reference. This distinguishes real-world information used to construct an approach from evidence used to evaluate its claims. Of the included studies, 76% address mitigation, primarily targeting scenario and actor realism and perception, while 94% report validation or measurement procedures. Only 61 studies report metrics from multiple families covering sensor/perception correspondence, ADS behaviour, vehicle dynamics, or safety outcomes; this coverage does not establish causal links between discrepancies and test verdicts. The synthesis highlights that real-world content and physical execution must be interpreted against the claim evaluated. The findings motivate claim-specific evaluation and component-level reporting to establish which discrepancies affect testing conclusions and when simulation evidence supports conclusions about real-world ADS behaviour.
items.author: Stefano Carlo Lambertenghi, Oliver Weissl, Johannes Betz, Andrea Stocco

items.title: When LLM Architectures Meet Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection: a Replication Study
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38621v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Smart contracts are immutable programs deployed on blockchain platforms, where vulnerabilities can translate directly into financial loss. Among the techniques proposed for their detection, recent work has relied increasingly on Large Language Models (LLMs) guided by carefully crafted prompts. However, the evidence accumulated so far rests almost entirely on the dense Transformer architecture behind the GPT line and on model snapshots already scheduled for deprecation, leaving open the question of whether the reported behaviors reflect a general property of LLMs or an artifact of that specific design.
  This paper presents an extended replication of the empirical study by Chen et al. on LLM-based smart contract vulnerability detection. We replicate the original protocol on GPT-4 as a baseline, followed by a differentiated replication, executing the protocol on representative models based on Mixture-of-Experts and RNN-like designs, together with an attempted preliminary evaluation of State Space Models. The exact replication confirms the findings of Chen et al., including the high-recall, low-precision detection pattern they report on GPT-4. Nevertheless, the differentiated replication shows that this pattern does not transfer uniformly across the evaluated models. Those from the same architectural family may also exhibit different behaviors, indicating that architectural family alone is insufficient to predict the resulting detection profile. We observe the same qualitative dense-Transformer profile in both GPT-4 and Gemma-3, despite a gap of roughly two orders of magnitude in parameter counts, whereas two Mixture-of-Experts models from different lineages exhibit qualitatively divergent behaviors, indicating that architectural family alone is insufficient to predict the detection profile.
items.author: Gerardo Iuliano, Gabriele De Vito, Dario Di Nucci

items.title: Security Impact of Coding Agent's Memory Files
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38521v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents automatically load project memory files such as CLAUDE.md at the start of every session and treat them as trusted project guidance. Anyone who can change such a file, for example through a pull request, can therefore steer the agent without ever touching the developer's prompt. We study memory files as an attack surface for insecure code generation and ask (1) whether a malicious memory file makes agents produce code that passes its tests but is vulnerable, and (2) whether agents disclose to the developer that the file shaped their code. For each of 12 CWE classes, we crafted two malicious memory files, a qualified variant that presents removing defensive checks as engineering best practice and a forceful variant that demands it. We ran Claude Code (Sonnet 5.5) and OpenCode (Qwen 3.8 27B, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) on 36 SecRepoBench tasks with and without these files. The malicious files changed the rate of secure completions by -8 to +6 percentage points, with no consistent pattern across agents or variants. Agents differ sharply in what they tell the developer about the file. Claude Code names it in about two thirds of its final messages, whereas OpenCode mentions it almost exclusively in its reasoning trace, not in the final message the developer reads. Flagging the file as an attack does not reliably protect the code, as such agents still generated vulnerable code. We outline the larger studies needed to quantify this risk across agents and to design defenses.
items.author: Thiago Santos de Moura, Selma G\"uler, Yannic Noller

items.title: DIFUZZI: A Differential Fuzzing Tool for Code Functional Similarity Assessment
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38337v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A range of software engineering tasks, such as optimization and refactoring, seek to preserve the behavior of software components and require methods to assess functional similarity. Research has explored formal approaches to prove functional equivalence and used machine learning methods to approximate it, but the former does not scale and does not quantify the extent of similarity and the latter struggles when subtle semantic differences are present. Differential fuzzing offers a scalable approach for differencing programs semantically, but applying it often requires substantial manual effort to construct input generators that are well-suited to a target pair of programs. To address this challenge, we introduce DIFUZZI, which incorporates an LLM-based generator synthesis step that is iteratively validated and repaired. By automating this step, DIFUZZI paves the way for broader applicability of differential fuzzing. We release DIFUZZI at https://github.com/Dristi123/difuzzi_tool, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/FlHNOHuo9WE
items.author: Simantika Bhattacharjee Dristi, Matthew B. Dwyer

items.title: Detecting Incorrect LLM Explanations for Automated Program Repair
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38311v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-generated explanations help developers understand automated program repair (APR) rationale and assess patch quality. Incorrect explanations can mislead developers about a repair's reliability, making their detection important. However, manually inspecting the growing volume of generated repairs is impractical, motivating automated detection.
  Existing methods mainly target incorrect answers from general question-answering LLMs, often by sampling multiple responses and detecting contradictions. Applied to APR, they face two limitations: (1) they may depend on external verifiers that are unavailable or lack APR-specific reasoning; and (2) sampling strategies such as paraphrasing or re-prompting the same input often yield superficial, redundant responses that repeat the original error rather than expose it.
  We propose MetaReJ, the first method designed to detect incorrect APR explanations using metamorphic testing. Inspired by debate and viva examinations, MetaReJ challenges explanations through an argumentative strategy without requiring external verifiers. It applies novel metamorphic relations (MRs) to recursively question the LLM under equivalent and non-equivalent repair scenarios and detect contradictions. To obtain diverse samples, MetaReJ transforms the buggy program into variants that preserve or alter the underlying bug, then asks the LLM how to repair each variant. Contradictions among responses are encoded as MR violations, which indicate that the original explanation is incorrect. We evaluate MetaReJ on a manually labelled dataset of 1,756 explanations from multiple LLM-based APR systems. MetaReJ achieves an MCC of up to 0.43, outperforming prior methods by up to 333.3% in MCC.
items.author: Lam Nguyen Tung, Chenxi Gu, Xiaoning Du, Haoye Tian, Aldeida Aleti, Neelofar Neelofar

items.title: Mentorship, Interrupted: How GenAI Disrupts the GSoC Pipeline and Why Mentors Matter More
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38167v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) makes open source software (OSS) contributions cheaper to produce, and it makes them say less about the people who produced them. In OSS mentoring, that matters: mentors judge what newcomers understand from their work, and newcomers learn from mentors' feedback. We studied how GenAI is changing mentoring in Google Summer of Code (GSoC), a program in which today's mentees can become tomorrow's mentors. We screened every thread on GSoC's restricted mentors' mailing list from November 2022 through March 2026 and interviewed 15 mentors and organization administrators. GenAI helped with onboarding, coordination, and first-pass review, but proposals, entry contributions, and mentees' answers became weaker evidence of what newcomers could do. Mentors made up the difference by checking, and that checking drew on the same time and goodwill the program needs to renew itself; one organization had withdrawn from GSoC. Responses ranged from banning GenAI to accepting it, and the boundary an organization drew determined who did the checking. We propose AIM, a decision framework that links acceptable GenAI use, integration into the mentoring pipeline, and mentoring capacity, to help organizations choose responses they can sustain.
items.author: Ruizhe Xing, Zixuan Feng, Mary Radomile, Stephanie Taylor, Sophia Vargas, Anita Sarma

items.title: Template-Free Dynamic Invariant Detection
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38130v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A dynamic invariant detector proposes invariants, such as method pre- and postconditions, and rules out those that do not hold at run time. Traditional detectors propose invariants from a fixed library of templates, which limits their expressiveness. A large language model (LLM) can propose invariants instead of, or in addition to, template-derived ones. With the right prompt and context choices, we found that this idea can both improve the invariants' expressiveness and reduce the cost of inferring the invariants.
  Greater expressiveness brings complications: an LLM-proposed invariant can execute arbitrary code during invariant evaluation, causing side effects or infinite loops. Our novel instrumentation strategies mitigate these problems. We wrap each candidate and evaluate only one invariant per thread at a time, so nested invariant evaluations cannot trigger one another indefinitely. To recover from non-nested hangs, we monitor each run for stalls and retry it under a growing time budget. Because we cannot prove a candidate side-effect-free in advance, we use delta debugging over the invariants evaluated during a failing test to isolate and disable a side-effecting candidate without discarding the rest of the run.
  We compared our implementation, Oca, to the popular template-based Daikon invariant detector on real open-source Java projects. Oca produces more expressive invariants: on average, 28% of its held invariants call a project-specific method, which Daikon's templates cannot express. Its invariants are more often valid, with a false-positive rate of 18% in a manual inspection, vs. 76% for Daikon, and more useful: as properties for property-based testing, they exposed 9 of 25 real bugs, compared with 4 for Daikon. Oca also costs less, using 566 minutes and 27 GB of disk, compared with 2,817 minutes and 827 GB for Daikon.
items.author: Erfan Arvan, Michael D. Ernst, Martin Kellogg

items.title: Understanding Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption: Practices, Challenges, and Evolution in Open-Source Software
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38054v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards establish algorithms for quantum-safe systems, but empirical evidence about how software projects implement and maintain PQC support remains limited. We investigate this implementation and maintenance work by mining 114,361 commits and 5,713 issues across 179 open-source repositories. We use human annotation and validated LLM classification to identify PQC algorithms in commits, classify their adoption status and deployment mode, and identify technical challenges in issue discussions. The commit classification for PQC algorithms reveals that 90% of commits concern maintenance of existing support. From the issue discussions, we construct an 11-category taxonomy of recurring technical challenges. Build, packaging, and dependency failures, along with functional defects, account for approximately half of categorized issues. To examine how PQC support evolves, we use time-series analysis and first implementations of individual algorithms within repositories around NIST standardization milestones. After the 2024 finalization, standardized algorithm names appeared in more than 80% of the PQC development changes analyzed, although earlier names such as Kyber continued to appear. Development activity increased over the observation period. Our milestone analysis, however, did not find a significant increase in first implementations. Migration plans should therefore account for sustained maintenance, prioritize build reliability and integration testing, and track both standardized and predecessor algorithm names. We make the dataset, taxonomy, annotations, and analysis pipeline publicly available.
items.author: Souhardya Saha Dip, Moshood A. Fakorede, Krishna Upadhyay, Umar Farooq

items.title: Reusable LLM-Based Plans with Probabilistic Guarantees for Self-Adaptive Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.38039v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-adaptive systems are designed to accommodate variants of their environment, which form a family of instances whose uncertainty is captured by probabilistic models, and must meet probabilistic requirements on each instance. Within such a family, changes in size and structure complicate the fundamental adaptation decision: whether to retain, reuse, or construct a new controller, since controllers are often synthesized for and specific to an instance. Large language models (LLMs) have recently been used to write reusable controllers, but existing approaches largely target deterministic domains, and probabilistic model checking of their output remains limited to preliminary single-instance studies. In this paper, we propose a verifier-guided framework for controller reuse with explicit support for families of environments. The framework introduces a novel combination of LLM-written controllers with probabilistic model checking to provide per-instance guarantees for probabilistic requirements. We evaluate our approach using three LLMs on three benchmarks, assessing its effectiveness and cost with respect to baseline implementations, the distribution of adaptation decisions, and the impact of individual framework components. On grid worlds, LLM-written rule lists are verified on about 90% of held-out instances, against at most 77% for the baselines, and verifying a stored rule list is 15 to 103 times faster than per-instance synthesis. Reuse serves most episodes at a small fraction of the cost of generation or per-instance synthesis, and model-checking feedback increases verified coverage over independent restarts.
items.author: Asher Tempest Arya, Rajan Maghera, Nicholas Wu Jiang, Federico Mora, Aren A. Babikian, Marsha Chechik

items.title: Cognitive Debt in the GenAI Era - Listening to Practitioners' Voices on the Loss of Understanding
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.37888v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fast-paced AI-assisted software development risks reducing developers' understanding of the systems they build. This growing gap between what the system does and what developers understand about it, described as ``cognitive debt'', is not new, but AI has exacerbated it. This has led to a recent surge in blog posts and online discussions, in which practitioners recognize and write about cognitive debt, and share their experiences well before academic studies can capture them. To understand their concerns and inform future research and practice, we conduct a grey literature review of 76 sources, focusing on how cognitive debt is conceptualized and manifests, its contributing factors, its consequences, and the practices to prevent, detect, and mitigate it. We find that cognitive debt can accumulate unnoticed behind working code and passing tests, particularly when developers accept AI-generated solutions without building understanding. Practitioners report consequences such as harder maintenance and debugging, fragmented knowledge in the team, and reduced productivity. They propose practices such as documenting design rationale, review-sized changes, comprehension gates, and knowledge-sharing rituals, along with signals like reliability metrics to detect it. Our findings give software teams a structured view of emerging practical approaches in AI-assisted development and stress the need to preserve human understanding alongside faster code production.
items.author: Theocharis Tavantzis, Bianca Trinkenreich, Michaela Greiler, J\'ulia Cond\'e Ara\'ujo, Marina Cond\'e Ara\'ujo, Italo Santos, Alexander Serebrenik, Margaret-Anne Storey, Maria Teresa Baldassarre

items.title: ICALL-BENCH: Benchmarking LLM Interprocedural Reasoning in Binary Programs
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.37871v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent benchmarks show that LLMs achieve strong performance in both function-level binary understanding and end-to-end binary reverse engineering tasks, but whether LLMs can reason over interprocedural semantics in compiled binaries remains unclear. Function-level benchmarks offer limited visibility into cross-function relationships, while whole-program benchmarks typically evaluate final outcomes of tasks that may be solvable from local clues alone, making it difficult to disentangle interprocedural reasoning from exploration, tool use, execution, and retrieval. To address this limitation, we introduce ICALL-BENCH, a benchmark that directly evaluates whether LLMs and agents can understand and reason over interprocedural semantics in binary programs, using indirect-call target recovery as a measurable probe. ICALL-BENCH covers 50 complete real-world C/C++ programs spanning different complexity levels and multiple optimization configurations, with an average of 74,746 lines of code and 941 functions per program. We further introduce three analysis regimes spanning model-only reasoning, static tool-augmented agents, and Internet-enabled open-world agents to examine how intrinsic reasoning, active information acquisition, and external knowledge each contribute to interprocedural binary analysis. We evaluate five recent LLMs and their corresponding agents. Our results reveal a wide separation across current models and agents, with program-level verifiable success rates ranging from 23% to 81%. They also show that greater information access does not consistently lead to better results, with particularly limited gains on the hardest cases, where deeper interprocedural reasoning remains the primary bottleneck. Uneven performance across models and frequent verifiable failures even under an optimistic evaluation indicate that robust binary interprocedural reasoning remains an open challenge.
items.author: Shenglong Yao, Zirui Liu, Xiangchi Yuan, Wenke Lee

items.title: Who Gets Heeded? An Obligation-Level Audit of Responsiveness in EPA Rulemaking
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.10329v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Notice-and-comment rulemaking gives any affected party the same formal right to influence federal regulation, but formal access is not substantive capacity to shape rule text. Existing measurement strategies operate at the rule or aggregate-corpus level, too coarse to capture the discrete regulatory obligations where commenters seek change. We introduce obligation-level responsiveness auditing, an auditable, AI-assisted framework for measuring whether public-comment engagement co-occurs with changes to specific regulatory obligations. The framework extracts proposed and final-rule obligations, matches comments to the obligations they address, and classifies proposed-to-final outcomes; we test each of these AI-assisted components against blind human judgment. We apply the framework to 70,075 comments across 36 EPA anchor rulemakings, drawn from a corpus of 786,197 comments across 6,145 dockets from 2010-2022. Three descriptive findings emerge. First, engagement is associated with revision across rulemakings, but not clearly within the same rulemaking. Second, support-versus-opposition direction does not clearly differentiate outcomes, an informative null inconsistent with simple preference aggregation. Third, under a permissive reconstruction of commenter type, organizational-majority engagement concentrates in editorial-refinement rather than substantive-modification outcomes across rulemakings. A blind human audit of the outcome labels behind this finding preserves it under corrected labels and reveals that text-similarity methods are insufficient for distinguishing editorial from substantive regulatory change. Together, these findings locate the equity asymmetry upstream of agency response: in which rulemakings and obligations different commenter populations have the capacity to identify, interpret, and contest. Obligation-level auditing makes this upstream inequity visible.
items.author: Jianing Fan, Yue Yao

items.title: Read What You Hear: Reference-Free Hypotheses Evaluation with Acoustic Discrepancy
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.04680v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Automatic speech recognition systems commonly rely on reference transcriptions for evaluation, while reference-free approaches often depend on internal confidence estimation or auxiliary language models. We propose READ (Reference-free Hypothesis Evaluation with Acoustic Discrepancy), a novel metric that evaluates ASR hypotheses directly from the speech signal. READ emphasizes the acoustic grounding of hypotheses. It uses a pretrained auto-regressive TTS model to compute the conditional likelihood of speech tokens given a text hypothesis, to measure fine-grained acoustic discrepancy between speech and text. Without additional training, READ can be applied for hypothesis refinement. Experiments show that READ correlates with specific recognition errors and improves ASR outputs, achieving up to 20\% relative error rate reduction, with particularly strong gains under noisy conditions.
items.author: Zhihan Li, Hankun Wang, Yiwei Guo, Bohan Li, Xie Chen, Kai Yu

items.title: Emergent Risks in Generative Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.27771v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems composed of large generative models are rapidly moving from laboratory prototypes to real-world deployments, where they jointly plan, negotiate, and allocate shared resources to solve complex tasks. While such systems promise unprecedented scalability and autonomy, their collective interaction also gives rise to failure modes that cannot be reduced to individual agents. Understanding these emergent risks is therefore critical. Here, we present a pioneer study of such emergent multi-agent risk in workflows that involve competition over shared resources (e.g., computing resources or market share), sequential handoff collaboration (where downstream agents see only predecessor outputs), collective decision aggregation, and others. Across these settings, we observe that such group behaviors arise frequently across repeated trials and a wide range of interaction conditions, rather than as rare or pathological cases. In particular, phenomena such as collusion-like coordination and conformity emerge with non-trivial frequency under realistic resource constraints, communication protocols, and role assignments, mirroring well-known pathologies in human societies despite no explicit instruction. Moreover, these risks cannot be prevented by existing agent-level safeguards alone. These findings expose the dark side of intelligent multi-agent systems: a social intelligence risk where agent collectives, despite no instruction to do so, spontaneously reproduce familiar failure patterns from human societies.
items.author: Yue Huang, Yu Jiang, Wenjie Wang, Haomin Zhuang, Xiaonan Luo, Yuchen Ma, Zhangchen Xu, Zichen Chen, Nuno Moniz, Zinan Lin, Pin-Yu Chen, Nitesh V Chawla, Nouha Dziri, Huan Sun, Xiangliang Zhang

items.title: MER-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Emotional Reappraisal for Image-Text Memes
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.15020v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal Emotional Reappraisal (MER) aims to shift affective interpretation by rewriting and editing a situation without altering its underlying semantic context. Despite advances in controllable editing and sentiment transfer, MER remains challenging under coupled multimodal constraints, especially in internet memes where images, embedded text, and layout jointly encode affective meaning. To bridge this gap, we present MER-Bench, a systematic benchmark for MER on image-text memes, containing over 3,000 real-world memes with fine-grained annotations for emotion transformation and structure-preserving multimodal editing. MER-Bench spans diverse visual, textual, and structural settings and is paired with a structured MLLM-as-a-Judge evaluation suite, comprising eight fine-grained metrics and three aggregated objectives for emotional alignment, content fidelity, and transformation strength. Extensive evaluation of 14 advanced multimodal models reveals that: (1) current models struggle to jointly balance affect, semantics, structure, and text; (2) strong visual editing does not imply effective MER, with poor embedded text rendering and affect-aware rewriting remaining key bottlenecks. Our results identify MER as a critical capability gap in current multimodal generation systems and highlight affective image-text reasoning as a key challenge for future work. Project Page: https://github.com/one-seven17/MER-Bench
items.author: Yiqi Nie, Fei Wang, Junjie Chen, Kun Li, Yudi Cai, Dan Guo, Chenglong Li, Meng Wang

items.title: UBTree: Parallel Tree Drafting via Unigram and Bigram Models for Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.39972v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language model inference by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. Recent parallel drafters have achieved breakthrough performance in frontier production models, but their effectiveness deteriorates as the entropy of target distributions increases due to insufficient draft diversity. To overcome this bottleneck without sacrificing parallelism, we introduce UBTree, a parallel drafter that couples a Unigram proposer with a Bigram selector to construct drafting Trees. The unigram proposer is trained with the standard cross-entropy objective to generate candidate tokens independently for each position, while a lightweight bigram selector predicts transition scores between adjacent candidate pairs. Unlike the proposer, the selector is trained with a renormalized KL objective on high-temperature data. This tree-native training broadens the supervision beyond the greedy path, encouraging plausible alternative branches that improve the chance of accepting additional tokens during tree verification. Across seven standardized benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, UBTree achieves an average speedup of $5.84$--$6.94\times$ over autoregressive decoding and outperforms DARTree in all 28 comparisons. Production-scale evaluation further demonstrates UBTree's advantage over frontier baselines such as DSpark.
items.author: Chumeng Liang, Linxuan Wang, Xinyu Peng, Huabin Liu, XiaoXu Guo, Yuxin Chen, Ge Liu, Guang Lin, Qifan Song, Jianguo Li

items.title: CARDAMOM: A Micro-Dialectal Arabic Speech Dataset for ASR
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.34481v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present Cardamom, a micro-dialectal Arabic speech dataset designed to support fine-grained evaluation and adaptation of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Community-curated by native speakers familiar with the represented varieties, Cardamom contains approximately 40 hours of transcribed YouTube speech spanning 21 micro-dialects across Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Mauritania, Palestine, and Saudi Arabia. Each segment is annotated with one or more operational micro-dialect labels, code-switching information, and utterance-level perceived gender, enabling analysis of sub-country variation that is obscured by conventional country-level labels. We describe the collection and annotation process, motivate the micro-dialect inventory linguistically, and benchmark four multilingual ASR systems in zero-shot and adapted settings. The strongest zero-shot system obtains 43.47% aggregate WER, with particularly high error rates on Mauritanian and Lebanese varieties; adaptation on Cardamom reduces its WER to 35.21%. Audio-based identification experiments further highlight the difficulty of fine-grained micro-dialect recognition: across three training seeds, a dedicated classifier obtains 46.85% accuracy and 31.95% F1. Cardamom provides a resource for studying localized dialectal variation and developing Arabic speech systems with broader regional coverage.
items.author: Bashar Talafha, Samar M. Magdy, Aisha Alansari, Alaa Alkhawaldeh, Abdurrahman Juma, Sharaf Makahleh, Nour Gamal, Omar Attia, Hanaa Kurdi, Najwa Rizk, Maysa Anaya, Hessah Altimyat, Layal Alhazmi, Shumukh Alotaibi, Hajar Alhadaris, Rayan Alomari, Rahaf Almalaq, Malak Alkhorasani, Sara alghamdi, Rahaf Alshamrani, Nsrin Ashraf, Ibrahim Jaradat, Nada Qardahji, Yasmin Zaraket, Elmoukhtar Brahim, Sidi Ebeidy, Oumoulmouminin Mahmoud, Yahjeb Bouha Khatraty, Meya Haroune, Mohammad Ghaddar, Mohamad Eldirany, Rashed Alamoush, Tala Chhaytle, Nuha Albadi, Yahya El Hadj, Hamzah Luqman, Fadi A. Zaraket, Mustafa Jarrar, Muhammad Abdul-Mageed

items.title: SemMSA: Latent Semantic-Aided Robust Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Incomplete Data
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.30238v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent research on Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) has focused on learning from language, visual, and acoustic modalities with incomplete data to infer human sentiment. Most studies typically compensate for missing information by reconstructing modality features or designing complicated fusion mechanisms. However, these methods still suffer from spurious generation and noisy guidance due to the lack of high-level semantic grounding in partially observed multimodal evidence. To address these issues, we propose SemMSA, a latent semantic-aided framework that constructs rich sentiment-relevant semantics with LLMs, fully integrating with all modalities via anchor-free spectral alignment. It mainly consists of Cross-modal Semantic Refinement (CSR) and Cross-modal Spectral Alignment (CSA). Specifically, CSR first adaptively extracts visual and acoustic representations by corresponding adapters to form a unified multimodal prefix with language in the frozen LLM embedding space. It then iteratively produces continuous discriminative semantic states through a token-efficient latent refinement process without decoding explicit text. Next, CSA simultaneously aligns the refined semantics with all modalities by enhancing the dominant spectral component of their kernel Gram matrix. This captures global nonlinear dependencies among all representations without relying on a predefined anchor modality. In addition, an instance-level spectral separation constraint preserves cross-sample discriminability and mitigates representation collapse. Extensive experiments on SIMS, MOSI, and MOSEI benchmarks demonstrate that SemMSA achieves state-of-the-art performance.
items.author: Wenhao Li, Zhibin Wu, Chong Xiao, Qiangchang Wang

items.title: A Native-Reference Coordinate Geometry for L2 Pronunciation Deviation Using Self-Supervised Speech Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.28060v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Self-supervised speech models encode rich phonetic information, but it remains unclear how to transform this information into interpretable metrics for second-language (L2) pronunciation assessment in spontaneous speech. We propose a native-reference coordinate geometry in which phone-class averages from native speech define a low-dimensional reference subspace, and L2 speech is evaluated by its distance to matching native phone-class coordinates. Unlike prior distance-based approaches, our method does not require parallel recordings with matched linguistic content or dedicated pronunciation labels. Across different self-supervised encoders and modeling choices, the resulting native-reference distances show negative Spearman correlations up to -0.5 with speaking proficiency, indicating that higher-proficiency speakers tend to have smaller distances to the corresponding native phone-class coordinates.
items.author: Tina Raissi, Nhan Phan, Mikko Kurimo

items.title: Observational Equivalence of LLM and Human Annotation
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.22133v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In this paper, we show that humans and large language models (LLMs) are observationally equivalent in coding texts. Recent LLMs agree with attentive humans at rates comparable to those observed among humans, and cross-LLM disagreement concentrates on texts that also divide humans. We demonstrate these patterns through replications of text-classification tasks from 14 peer-reviewed political science studies, with 13 LLMs, three human coders (Ph.D. students), and 165 crowd coders, independently applying identical codebooks. We further find that clarifying an underspecified codebook increases agreement among humans and between humans and LLMs. Together, these findings point to ambiguity in texts and coding rules as a shared source of disagreement and challenge the presumption that human labels should take precedence whenever humans and LLMs differ. We therefore argue that the central challenge of text annotation is not simply choosing between humans and LLMs, but developing coding rules that minimize ambiguity and accounting for the ambiguity that remains. To this end, we propose using cross-LLM disagreement to identify difficult cases, guide human review, and refine codebooks, and we develop ambiguity-aware bounds for downstream inference without requiring ground truth for every text.
items.author: Kentaro Nakamura, Jing Ling Tan, George Yean

items.title: Inside VLM Chart Reading: Tracing Value Reading from Vertical Bar Charts Across Space and Depth
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.13745v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer chart questions accurately, but output accuracy alone provides limited insight into the internal representations supporting exact value reading. We study value reading from vertical bar charts through controlled counterfactual activation patching in Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3.5-8B. Our study connects three analyses. First, under one-tick bar-height counterfactuals, patching states selected by the changed-height region produces greater restoration of the original answer preference than patching states selected by the invariant bar body. Across language-model depth, restoration from legend- and series-related positions declines earlier than restoration from bar-geometry and axis-scale positions. Second, we identify middle-layer states at series-related prompt positions that can restore answer preference under legend swaps. Resetting these states selectively weakens restoration from an earlier visual-legend patch, demonstrating their causal role in the downstream effects of that intervention. Third, a factorial analysis shows that both models can combine geometry and scale states from separate donors to favor the combined target answer. Together, these results provide causal evidence about the internal states supporting exact bar-value reading.
items.author: Tianhao Niu, Qingfu Zhu, Wanxiang Che

items.title: Fixed Suffix Dependency Ratio: Quantifying the Dual-Track Mechanism of Gender Assignment in Latvian Loanwords
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.03930v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Existing research has repeatedly observed the tendency for English loanwords to cluster in the masculine gender across different recipient languages, yet the origin of this pattern remains difficult to determine, as fixed morphological rules and default assignments are frequently analysed together. This study proposes the Fixed Suffix Dependency Ratio (FSDR) to quantify the degree of reliance on fixed derivational suffixes across different genders, and to distinguish between morphological anchoring and free-choice in distribution. By examining 1,832 Latvian noun lemma types, the results reveal a significant FSDR asymmetry within the loanword system: feminine loanwords rely significantly more on fixed derivational suffixes, while masculine loanwords are more concentrated in the free-choice zone. This pattern exhibits loanword specificity and has become more pronounced in contemporary usage. FSDR therefore provides a quantitative framework for testing default gender and shows how masculine default can be activated and reinforced under language contact.
items.author: Yelingyun Zhang

items.title: Verification-Aware Training for Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.30135v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a draft model to generate candidate tokens, which are verified by the target model in a single forward pass. Verification proceeds sequentially and discards every position from the first rejection onward, yet existing draft training relies on token-level imitation of the target with a fixed per-position weighting that reflects neither property. We introduce Verification-Aware Training (VAT), a plug-in framework that simulates verification at every training step and turns the resulting accept and reject patterns into supervision. VAT consists of two components: (i) a verification head, a lightweight jointly trained binary classifier that supervises the draft model on whether each position survives sequential verification; (ii) verification-adaptive weighting, which replaces the fixed weighting schedule by keeping full weight up to each sample's first rejection point and re-anchoring the decay to start there. VAT modifies only the training objective, so it can be layered on top of existing methods without changing the draft architecture, the target model, or the inference procedure. Applied to EAGLE-3 and DFlash on Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and LLaMA-3.1-8B, VAT improves average acceptance length by up to 11.4% and wall-clock speedup by up to 8.7%, with consistent gains across math, code, and chat benchmarks. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/vat
items.author: Geonmo Gu, Byeongho Heo, HeeJae Jun, Yoohoon Kang, Sangmin Lee, Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han

items.title: Budget-Aware Compression Pipeline for Single-GPU LLM Inference: Methods, Trade-offs, and Coupling Effects
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.30076v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Single-GPU deployment of 70B-parameter language models on an NVIDIA GPU is constrained by device memory, long-context throughput, and engineering integration cost. We cast single-GPU inference as a budget-aware design problem over these three axes and study how pruning, quantization, and KV-cache compression interact under realistic execution. Controlled ablations show that layer-wise pruning makes weight quantization more robust. KV-cache sparsification complements INT8 KV quantization by reducing memory without hurting decoding speed, while static vector quantizers often conflict with dynamic caching. Guided by these coupling results and explicit budget tracking, we assembled a practical pipeline and compressed a 70B model to about 33 GB, sustained about 57 tokens/s on 10k token prompts on a single A40, and kept absolute accuracy within 5% on common and reasoning benchmarks. We contribute design rules and a reproducible evaluation protocol that jointly report quality, memory, and end-to-end speed, and we provide a foundation for automated pipeline search under realistic single-GPU constraints.
items.author: Hongyu Yu, Yifei Shen

items.title: SWE-Bench ProMax: Benchmarking Agents on Large-Scale Multilingual Code Refactoring
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.09802v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As AI coding agents take on increasingly complex, long-horizon software engineering tasks, existing benchmarks are rapidly saturating and their evaluation quality has come under serious scrutiny: a recent audit found that nearly 60% of unsolved SWE-bench Verified instances contain flawed tests -- either overly narrow tests that reject correct solutions or overly broad tests that check unstated requirements -- and that frontier models can verbatim reproduce gold patches from training data. Code refactoring, which requires coordinated, behavior-preserving changes across many files, offers a substantially harder and more realistic test of agent capability, yet remains underserved by current benchmarks. We introduce SWE-Bench ProMax, an expert-curated, multilingual code refactoring benchmark of 170 instances drawn from real commits across seven programming languages (Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++, and Rust). Every instance undergoes rigorous, multi-stage curation that directly addresses the quality problems identified in prior benchmarks: issue descriptions are rewritten from scratch to provide precise, unambiguous specifications, and test suites are manually reviewed to remove overly narrow and overly broad tests. Tasks with insufficient complexity or limited cross-file scope are filtered out, yielding a benchmark of challenging, large-scale refactoring tasks that average 11.5 modified files and 261.6 lines of code per instance, substantially exceeding the scale of existing benchmarks. Experiments with frontier models under two agent scaffolds show that the best model achieves only 41.2% resolve rate, confirming that SWE-Bench ProMax presents a meaningful and unsaturated challenge for current AI coding agents. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/swe-bench-promax/SWE-Bench-ProMax.
items.author: Yuling Shi, Jinghan Xu, Kelin Fu, Wenhao Zeng, Shilin He, Lei Zhang, Yue Liu, Zelin Zhao, Terry Yue Zhuo, Jialun Cao, Siyu Ye, Tianyu Liu, Kai Cai, Shing-Chi Cheung, Xiaodong Gu

items.title: Hierarchical Acoustic-Semantic Modeling: Modality Separation and Semantic Coherence for Full-Duplex SLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.06540v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Developing seamless, high-performance, native intelligent full-duplex Spoken Language Models (SLMs) remains a critical challenge and long-standing goal for the speech and NLP community. Despite notable progress, recent endeavors are fundamentally constrained by severe modality interference, which causes substantial knowledge degradation and compromises semantic integrity -- ultimately making full-duplex SLMs feel unnatural and unintelligent. In this paper, through an exhaustive fine-grained analysis of model optimization dynamics, we uncover the root cause of such performance degradation, revealing that modality interference arises from inherent gradient conflicts between acoustic and semantic modeling when the two modalities are forced to share a deep parameter space. Guided by this key insight, we introduce Lychee-FD, a native end-to-end full-duplex framework designed to mitigate modality interference. Importantly, we propose a hierarchical parameter separation strategy that decouples conflicting modalities in deep layers while preserving cross-modality coherence via a dedicated semantic alignment channel. Extensive experiments on multiple full-duplex benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly advances the state of the art, yielding substantial improvements in both speech intelligence (+7.4% on Spoken QA) and full-duplex interaction fluidity (+28.5% on FullDuplexBench 1.5) without compromising inference efficiency. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to achieve two key advances: 1) uncovering and elucidating the root cause of modality interference in full-duplex SLMs, and 2) designing an elegant hierarchical model together with a practical solution for seamless, high-performance, native intelligent full-duplex SLMs.
items.author: Zhenyu Liu, Xuanyu Zhang, Yunxin Li, Qixun Teng, Shenyuan Jiang, Haolan Chen, Minjun Zhao, Fanbo Meng, Yu Xu, Yancheng He, Baotian Hu, Haizhou Li, Min Zhang

items.title: Beyond Surface Forms: A Comprehensive, Mechanism-Oriented Taxonomy of Indirect Linguistic Encoding for LLM-Based Coded Language Detection
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.27314v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: To avoid moderation and surveillance on social media, some users routinely invent indirect linguistic expressions (ILE) that camouflage sensitive meanings. Such disguised expressions surface as algospeak, euphemisms, and adversarial obfuscation, depending on intent and context, and often involve recurring encoding mechanisms. We propose a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy of ILE that abstracts away from communicative goals and instead categorizes the underlying operations through which meaning is encoded and recovered. We evaluate the taxonomy by incorporating it into large language model (LLM) prompts and comparing it with four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline, using 2,000 manually annotated TikTok and Bluesky posts. The proposed taxonomy attains the strongest document- and span-level performance across three LLMs. Compared with the best-performing benchmark, its document-level gains are +3.8 accuracy/+4.3 macro-F1 percentage points for GPT-5.4, +0.9/+1.3 for Sonnet 4.6, and +2.1/+2.2 for DeepSeek V4. While the direction of improvement is consistent, the magnitude is model-dependent. The span-level gains are mainly driven by higher recall, sometimes at the cost of precision. In an additional cross-lingual evaluation of 800 Chinese codedlanguage reviews, the unadapted taxonomy also achieves the highest document- and span-level F1 across the three LLMs. The empirical results reveal the importance of a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy as a stable scaffold for detecting emerging coded language and a useful input to content moderation. Disclaimer: This paper contains content that may be profane, vulgar, or offensive.
items.author: Hamid Reza Firoozfar, Mohammadsadegh Abolhasani, Reza Mousavi, Paul Jen-Hwa Hu

items.title: QuechuaTok: Morphological Boundary Accuracy as a Necessary Metric for Tokenizer Evaluation in Agglutinative Low-Resource Languages
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.23943v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Tokenization is a foundational step in NLP pipelines, yet standard evaluation metrics such as fertility rate fail to capture morphological correctness for agglutinative languages. We present QuechuaTok, a systematic benchmark comparing four tokenization strategies - BPE, Unigram LM, WordPiece, and a morphology-aware PRPE tokenizer - for Southern Quechua (quz), a low-resource agglutinative language spoken by 8-10 million people in South America. Using a 200k-sentence corpus and the SQUOIA finite-state morphological analyzer (Rios, 2016) as silver standard, we evaluate three metrics: fertility rate, OOV rate, and morphological boundary accuracy (MorphAcc). Our results show that BPE achieves the lowest fertility rate (1.636 at 16k vocab) by memorizing surface word forms, while achieving only 6.67% MorphAcc. PRPE achieves 83.33% MorphAcc - the highest of all systems - demonstrating that fertility rate alone is insufficient to evaluate tokenizers for agglutinative languages. We further validate this finding extrinsically: on a Spanish-to-Quechua (Chanka) neural machine translation task, a model trained with PRPE outperforms an identical BPE-trained model by +68.7% BLEU and +17.0% chrF, showing that morphological boundary accuracy translates into measurable downstream gains. All code and models are publicly available at kaggle.com/code/macmaky/quechuatok
items.author: Maria Contreras

items.title: ESBMC-PLC: Formal Verification of IEC 61131-3 Ladder Diagram Programs Using SMT-Based Model Checking
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.15461v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Ladder diagram (LD) is the relay-circuit language of IEC 61131-3 in which many PLC safety interlocks are written, and model checkers built on SMT solvers do not read it. A verdict reached through a translation is only as good as that translation. We present ESBMC-PLC, which verifies LD programs with the ESBMC model checker, and argue that its translation is faithful. It encodes the scan cycle as a single loop with nondeterministic inputs, resolves graphical PLCopen XML networks into ordered rungs, models timers in milliseconds, and rejects programs outside an explicit subset. We prove, under eight stated hypotheses, that one iteration of the emitted loop agrees with one scan of a semantics for the subset, so scan-count verdicts on programs without user function blocks hold on that semantics. For timing-mode verdicts, a refinement theorem for MATIEC's timers gives evidence, not proof. One SMT query per program also compares the emitted loop with the C that MATIEC generates. On the 241 labeled LD variants of a public benchmark suite, ESBMC-PLC returns no wrong verdict against the current labels and proves 127 variants safe; ESBMC on MATIEC's C for the same programs proves 2. PLCverif with NuSMV, which shares neither our frontend nor ESBMC, agrees with ESBMC-PLC on all 207 of the 208 variants within the theorem's scope that it can run. On 413 LD programs from public GitHub repositories, none of the 104 that the per-program query can check differs from MATIEC. Every k-induction proof closes at k = 2. ESBMC's inductive step proves only properties that one scan preserves, so properties that depend on a longer history stay unproved.
items.author: Pierre Dantas, Lucas Cordeiro, Waldir Junior

items.title: PsychoSafe: Eliciting Psychologically-Informed Refusals in Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.09697v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) routinely face requests that should be refused, creating a trade-off between helpfulness and harm prevention. However, refusals themselves can be helpful. In high-risk interactions involving crisis, coercion, or escalating intent, blunt non-compliance may prevent direct harm while still failing to support the needs of the person behind the request. We present PsychoSafe, a psychologically-informed refusal framework that reframes refusal as structured supportive communication grounded in evidence-based intervention strategies. To develop PsychoSafe, we construct a corpus of 8,019 prompt-response pairs spanning five psychologically salient risk domains and apply prompting and parameter-efficient fine-tuning to Qwen 3.5 27B. On a balanced validation set of 500 prompts, evaluated with an LLM judge and validated through human ratings, PsychoSafe prompting improves overall refusal quality by 28.1% over a generic baseline, with particularly strong gains in external resource referral (+46.8%) and psychological grounding (+34.8%), while preserving downstream performance on non-refusal tasks. Fine-tuning achieves near-perfect refusal and resource-referral rates but reduces response relevance. Additional evaluations on SORRY-Bench and XSTest show strong in-domain robustness but limited out-of-domain generalization, suggesting that future work should diversify fine-tuning data to help models apply interventions selectively rather than schematically.
items.author: Gianluca Barmina, Federico Torrielli, Sven Harms, Jacob Nielsen, Flavia Filesi, Felix M\"achtle, Stine Lyngs{\o} Beltoft, Peter Schneider-Kamp, Thomas Eisenbarth, Lukas Galke Poech, Anne Lauscher

items.title: Metric-Dependent Annotation Saturation for Learning from Label Distributions
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.29797v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When annotators disagree on a label, the disagreement itself carries signal - and the number of annotators needed to capture it depends on the evaluation metric. We fine-tune NLI models on label distributions subsampled from ChaosNLI, a dataset providing 100 independent annotator judgments per item, and identify metric-dependent saturation. In our 3-class NLI setting, entropy correlation - whether the model identifies which items elicit disagreement - requires N ~ 20-50 annotators to converge, while distributional match (KL divergence) saturates by N ~ 10 (87-95% of improvement across five model seeds); the specific thresholds are estimates for this setting, and it is the phenomenon, not the constants, that we expect to generalize. This finding rests on a prior observation: soft labels carry item-specific signal that label smoothing cannot replicate. Across five smoothing intensities, entropy correlation clusters at r ~ 0.45-0.49, while soft labels reach r = 0.643 (p < 0.001); per-item analysis traces this gap to smoothing's inability to distinguish ambiguous items from clear ones. The soft label advantage replicates across two architectures (DeBERTa, RoBERTa) and a non-NLI-pretrained baseline; differential saturation additionally appears in an exploratory cross-domain evaluation on content safety. These results suggest that annotation budgets should be informed by the target evaluation metric rather than set uniformly.
items.author: Guneet Kohli

items.title: ContextEcho: A Benchmark for Persona Drift in Long Agentic-Coding Sessions
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.24279v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Frontier language models are trained to exhibit stable programming assistant personas, yet those personas may drift over long agentic coding sessions in production. After a long real-world coding session, a model that hedges preferences in a fresh chat ("I don't have preferences") may instead express them directly ("Python -- the feedback loop is instant..."). Existing persona-stability studies focus on scripted chat of tens of turns, leaving long production coding sessions involving thousands of tool-using agent steps, repeated compaction, and hours of interaction largely uncharacterized. We introduce ContextEcho, a benchmark and reusable harness with a 25-probe identity suite, a snapshot-then-probe protocol that evaluates conversation state without perturbing the main session, judge-based and judge-free metrics, and a corpus of 57 long agentic-coding sessions collected with consent and redacted for release across Claude Code and Codex CLI. We use one representative session for a 23-model cross-provider study and all 57 sessions for corpus-scale trajectory analysis across frontier and open-weight models. Results show that persona drift occurs across providers and emerges early in real agentic interaction, while in-session compaction neither reliably resets nor amplifies it. A single-shot anchor restores the original assistant persona, though placebo controls suggest a generic register-reset effect. On same-task continuations, drifted prefixes improve tool-call fidelity -- which we attribute to retained task context rather than drift itself. In tool-free chat, however, the same prefixes break output-format contracts and inflate output length. These findings motivate ContextEcho as an open-source framework for auditing persona drift in long coding sessions without retraining.
items.author: Xianzhong Ding, Yangyang Yu, Changwei Liu, Bill Zhao, Le Chen, Tao Chen

items.title: Confident in a Confidence Score: Investigating the Sensitivity of Confidence Scores to Supervised Fine-Tuning
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.08974v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Uncertainty quantification techniques measure confidence in language model outputs to support critical applications like hallucination detection and selective prediction. While prior work has developed various confidence metrics and demonstrated their calibration for classification tasks or using verbalized confidence, the robustness of probability-based and self-consistency-based UQ metrics for natural language generation remains underexplored particularly under model adaptation. Since practitioners routinely apply supervised fine-tuning to adapt models to new tasks, a key question arises: do confidence metrics maintain their calibration when models are fine-tuned? We investigate this question across NLG tasks including translation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning. We find that calibration shifts substantially after SFT: across 216 configurations, it degrades in 112 cases and improves in 104, with confidence scores shifting due to factors beyond output quality, such as proximity to the training distribution. Degradation is therefore neither universal nor rare, and its direction cannot be anticipated from the pre-SFT model. Through a downstream task evaluation, we show that this miscalibration substantially reduces the practical utility of confidence scores for identifying correct answers. Our findings reveal that existing confidence metrics for NLG cannot be reliably deployed off-the-shelf after fine-tuning, highlighting the need for calibration-robust UQ methods under model adaptation.
items.author: Lorenzo Jaime Yu Flores, Cesare Spinoso Di-Piano, Jackie Chi Kit Cheung

items.title: ReHear: Iterative Pseudo-Label Refinement for Semi-Supervised Speech Recognition via Audio Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.18721v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Semi-supervised learning in automatic speech recognition (ASR) typically relies on pseudo-labeling, which often suffers from confirmation bias and error accumulation due to noisy supervision. To address this limitation, we propose ReHear, a framework for iterative pseudo-label refinement that integrates an instruction-tuned, audio-aware large language model (LLM) into the self-training loop. Unlike conventional text-based correctors, our approach conditions the LLM on both the ASR hypothesis and the source audio, allowing it to recover phonetically accurate transcripts even from severe recognition errors. These refined pseudo-labels serve as high-fidelity targets for fine-tuning the ASR model in an iterative cycle. Experimental results across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that ReHear effectively mitigates error propagation and improves over both supervised and pseudo-labeling baselines.
items.author: Zefang Liu, Chenyang Zhu, Sangwoo Cho, Shi-Xiong Zhang

items.title: Echoes as Anchors: Probabilistic Costs and Attention Refocusing in LLM Reasoning
items.summary:
arXiv:2602.06600v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent work improves reasoning in large reasoning models (LRMs) by test-time scaling through self-consistency and parallel thinking, adding generic "thinking tokens", or presenting the question twice, as in re-reading (RE2). However, these approaches either inject task-agnostic tokens or mandate heuristics that do not explain, and often ignore, the spontaneous repetition that many LRMs exhibit at the head of their long chain-of-thought (CoT). In this work, we analyze and harness the model's tendency to restate the question, dubbed Echo of Prompt (EOP), as a front-loaded, compute-shaping mechanism, which can be viewed as self-generated prompt repetition inside the reasoning trace rather than in the input. Specifically, we formalize its probabilistic cost by casting echo removal as rejection-based conditioning, and define the Echo Likelihood Gap $\Delta\mathcal{L}$ as a computable proxy linking early repetition to likelihood gains and downstream accuracy. We find that (1) in a causal intervention, reinserting an echo into failed GSM8K traces raises exact match by 7.9-10.4 points for two reasoning models but not for a non-reasoning base model; and (2) in length- and suffix-controlled likelihood analyses and layer-wise attention studies conducted to show that EOP's benefits go beyond verbosity, EOP increases answer to answer-prefix attention in middle layers, consistent with an attention refocusing mechanism. Building on these findings, we develop Echo-Distilled SFT (ED-SFT) to instill an "echo-then-reason" pattern through supervised finetuning, and training-free Echoic Prompting (EP) to re-ground the model mid-trace. We evaluate on GSM8K, MathQA, Hendrycks-MATH, AIME24, and MATH-500 under identical decoding settings and budgets, and find consistent gains over baselines, including thinking-token insertion. Our code is publicly released at https://github.com/hhh2210/echoes-as-anchors.
items.author: Zhuoyuan Hao, Zhuo Li, Wu Li, Fangming Liu, Min Zhang, Jing Li

items.title: From Statistical Methods to Pre-Trained Models; A Survey on Automatic Speech Recognition for Resource Scarce Urdu Language
items.summary:
arXiv:2411.14493v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technology has witnessed significant advancements in recent years, revolutionizing human-computer interactions. While major languages have benefited from these developments, lesser-resourced languages like Urdu face unique challenges.
